propname: AASHTO GROUP INDEX NUMBER THICKEST LAYER IN DEPTH 10-40 in.
description:
Finds the AASHTO Group Index for the thickest horizon that has any portion in the depths 10" to 40" (25 to 100 cm) or above bedrock.  Portions outside the depth range are not considered in the  horizon thickness.

Returns values for low, high, and rv: normally each has a single value.

propname: AASHTO GIN THICKEST LAYER IN DEPTH
description:

Returns values for low, high, and rv: normally each has a single value.

Computes the total of Available Water Capacity from the surface to the first restrictive layer, or to the bottom of the last defined horizon if there are no restrictive layers.  The total is computed by multiplying the horizon AWC by the horizon thickness for that portion of each horizon in the depth range, them summing across horizons.

Returns values for low, high, and rv: each has a single value.

Computes the total of Available Water Capacity from the surface to the first restrictive layer, or to 40" (100 cm), whichever is first. Returns values for low, high, and rv: each has a single value.

propname: CALCIUM CARBONATE  THICKEST LAYER IN DEPTH 0-100CM
description:
Finds the value of Calcium Carbonate Equivalent for the thickest horizon that has any portion in the depths 0" to 40" (0 to 100 cm) or to a restrictive layer.  Portions outside the depth range are not considered in the horizon thickness.
 
Returns values for low, high, and rv: normally each has a single value; if horizons tie for thickest, a value will be returned for each.

Computes the weighted average of the ratio CEC / Clay %.  Computed by multiplying the CEC / Clay ratio for each horizon by the horizon thickness to the total profile depth, and summing across all horizons.
 
Returns a single value for the rv only:  The high and low values that result from this calculation are meaningless because these calculations result is numbers that are not monotonic in nature.  In some cases the low is greater than either the high or the rv.  In others the rv is greater than the low and high calculation and in other cases the high is greater than the low but less than the rv.  Upon analysis of the intent and purpose of this property in relation to the interpretive evaluation and rule the decision was made to use the rv only.  Bob Nielsen 7/98.

Computes the weighted average of the ratio CEC / Clay %.  Computed by multiplying the CEC / Clay ratio for each horizon by the ratio of the horizon thickness to a depth of 50cm.
 
Returns a single value for the rv only:  The high and low values that result from this calculation are meaningless because these calculations result is numbers that are not monotonic in nature.  In some cases the low is greater than either the high or the rv.  In others the rv is greater than the low and high calculation and in other cases the high is greater than the low but less than the rv.  Upon analysis of the intent and purpose of this property in relation to the interpretive evaluation and rule the decision was made to use the rv only.  Bob Nielsen 7/98.

Computes the percentage of all rock fragments greater than 2mm in size in the surface horizon.  Uses sieve and rock percents from the Horizon table.
 
The 2mm to 3" fragments are represented by the percent retained on the #10 sieve (100 - #10). This is adjusted for stones by multiplying it times the fraction less than 3" (1 - (Rock 3-10 + Rock >10)/100).
Then the percentages for rocks 3" to 10", and rocks > 10", are added on to determine the total fragments > 2mm.

Returns values for low, high, and rv: each has a single value.

Finds the lowest value for permeability (K-Sat) in horizons that have any portion in the depth range 20" to 60" (50-150 cm).

Returns values for low, high, and rv: each has a single value.

Data used:  hzdept_r, hzdepb_r, frag3to10_l, frag3to10_h, frag3to10_r, fraggt10_l, fraggt10_h and fraggt10_r from  the component, component horizon, and component restrictions tables.
	Considerations:
	1.  Depth to the top of the first restrictive layer;
	2.  Horizon depth;
	3.  Percent coarse fragments > 3 inches.

Logic:  Finds the weighted average percentage of rock fragments of size greater than 75mm in the horizons above a restrictive feature or from 0 to 180 cm deep.  Uses the rock percents from the Horizon table.

To compute a weighted average, the sum of rock  > 75mm for each horizon is multiplied by the horizon thickness, then averaged over all horizons above a restrictive feature or to 150cm.

Returns values for low, high, and rv: each has a single value.

Data used:  hzdept_r, sieveno10_l, sieveno10_h, sieveno10_r, frag3to10_l, frag3to10_h, frag3to10_r, fraggt10_l, fraggt10_h and fraggt10_r from  the component, component horizon, and component restrictions tables.
	Considerations:
	1.  Depth to the top of the first restrictive layer;
	2.  Horizon depth;
	3.  Percent Passing the 10# sieve and
	4.  Percent coarse fragments > 3 inches.

Logic:  Finds the rv weighted average of rock fragments of size 2mm to <75mm  in all horizons above a  restrictive layer or within 150cm  of the surface.  Uses sieve and rock percents from the Horizon table.  Selects depth from horizons whose upper depth above a restrictive layer is within the 0 to 150 cm depth.  For horizons extending below 150 cm, the weighted average may be biased.

The 2mm to <75mm fragments are represented by the percent retained on the #10 sieve (100 - #10). This is adjusted for stones by multiplying it times the fraction less than 75mm (1 - (Rock 3-10 + Rock >10)/100).


Returns values for low, high, and rv: each has a single value.

Script as originally written assigned all unifieds to low and high. Therefore

 low and high may or may not be gravel. To overcome this oddity regarding the range, 
 I changed script to rv only (commented out the low and high; modified the rv).

Script as currently written only keeps horizons with unifieds. Therefore R, Cr,
 and *f*/mat horizons are not part of selected set. That is why it outputs data
 for the horizon above the bedrock or permafrost horizon. This works but only luck
 would have it, as opposed to keeping all horizons and then outputting data for the
 horizon above the bedrock or permafrost.

description:
dmoore 3/28/00  major twicking to try and match legacy.  Tested against Matsu (some "slight" ratings will change to "very limited" where stratified soils with sandy textures occure), North Star, Gerstle, Copper River, Upper Tanana, and Yentna.  With mostly good results, except where noted in Matsu and where legacy ratings for stratified textures, i.e., SR-S-SIL were inconsistent.  Some times legacy would rate these textures "severe" other times too sandy rating was not addressed.

Phone call with Bob Neilsen on 3/29/00 on this matter.  At this time Bob could not give a reason for legacy inconsistenties with rating stratified soils with sandy layers.  He hopes to have an answer sometime in the future.

Changed rule rating name from Too sandy to Too sandy, caving.  Phone call with Bob Neilsen on this matter.  Bob could not give reason why to have too sandy rating unless it was for cutbanks caving or trench wall strenght.  He hopes to have an answer sometime in the future.  Made rule name rating change to keep orginal too sandy criteria as opposed to replacing it with the cutbank caving in shallow excavations.

Edited 7/12/2010 By Jesse Turk. replaced the subquery with criteria in the where clause since the base table will take care of any coordination. Original Script:
BASE TABLE component.
 
# Get the first representative horizon top depth where hpm, mpm and spm textures do not exist.
 
EXEC SQL select hzdept_r
FROM component, chorizon WHERE
JOIN component TO chorizon AND
NOT EXISTS(select * from chtexturegrp, component, chorizon where
JOIN component TO chorizon AND
JOIN chorizon TO chtexturegrp and 
texture IN("HPM", "MPM", "SPM"));
SORT by hzdept_r
AGGREGATE COLUMN hzdept_r FIRST.

Generates an ecological site name by combining the fields of the Ecological Site table into a string, which is returned in a variable named ecositenm. It requires the record id of the Ecological Site as a parameter. For example:

DERIVE ecositenm USING "NSSC Pangaea":"Ecological Site Name" (ecositeiid).

The rules for generating the name are:

If the Ecological Site Primary Name is non-blank, the Secondary and Tertiary names (if used) are appended to the Primary name with a space between each. This will be used as the output of the property.

If the Ecological Site Tree 1 is non-blank, the Tree, Shrub and Herb species are concantenated. If there are two trees the species names are combined with a hyphen, like "pine-spruce". If only one of the tree species is listed no hyphen is used. The pairs of shrub and herb species are combined the same way. Then the non-blank results of that step are combined with a slash "/" delimiter to produce the ecological site name. Examples are:

tree1-tree2/shrub1-shrub2/herb1-herb2
tree1/shrub1/herb1
tree1-tree2/shrub1

If both the Primary Name and Tree 1 columns have data, the corect form of the result cannot be determined and the result is set to "ambiguous name". If both columns are blank, even if other columns are filled in, the result is blank.

Then the percentages for rocks 3" to 10", and rocks > 10", are added on to determine the total fragments > 2mm.

Returns values for low, high, and rv: each has a single value.

Applications:
  Designed for use as a indicator of relative erosion rate in soil degredation interpretations.
  
Limitations:
  Does not adjust for the Palouse region.
  Does not consider rainfall, cropping, or practice factors.
  Does not apply to organic soils.
  Not a predictor of actual erosion rate.

Citations:
  USDA Ag Handbook 537.

Logic: Finds the average percentage of rock fragments of size greater than 3" in the horizons from 0" to 40" (0 to 100 cm) deep or first restrictive layer.  Uses the rock percents from the Horizon table.  To compute a weighted average, the sum of rock 3-10" and rock > 10" for each horizon is multiplied by the horizon thickness, then averaged over all horizons to 40".

Data used: awc from component horizon table.
	Consideration:
	1.  AWC
	2.  DEPTH TO FIRST WATER OR ROOT RESTRICTIVE LAYER or 100cm
	3.  Layer Thickness
	
Logic: Computes the total of Available Water Capacity from the surface to the first water and root restrictive layer, or to the bottom of the last defined horizon if there are no restrictive layers.  The total is computed by multiplying the horizon AWC by the horizon thickness for that portion of each horizon in the depth range, them summing across horizons.

Returns values for low, high, and rv: each has a single value.

	1.  CEC-7 OR ECEC
	2.  Layer Thickness 0 to 200cm
	3.  "NSSC Pangaea": LAYER THICKNESS IN RANGE; ABOVE A RESTRICTIVE LAYER
	
Logic: Computes the weighted average of the ratio CEC / Clay %.  Computed by multiplying the CEC / Clay ratio for each horizon by the ratio of the horizon thickness to a depth of 100 cm or a restrictive layer, which ever is less.
 
Returns values for low, high, and rv: each has a single value.

propname: COARSE FRAGMENTS 2 to 75MM IN DEPTH 0 TO 60CM, MAXIMUM (TX)
description:
Data used:  hzdept_r, sieveno10_l, sieveno10_h, sieveno10_r, frag3to10_l, frag3to10_h, frag3to10_r, fraggt10_l, fraggt10_h and fraggt10_r from  the component, component horizon, and component restrictions tables.
	Considerations:
	1.  Depth to the top of the first restrictive layer;
	2.  Horizon depth;
	3.  Percent Passing the 10# sieve and
	4.  Percent coarse fragments > 3 inches.

Logic:  Finds the layer with the maximum rock fragments of size 2mm to <75mm  within 60cm of the surface.  Uses sieve and rock percents from the Horizon table.  Selects depth from horizons whose upper depth is <= 60cm.

The 2mm to <75mm fragments are represented by the percent retained on the #10 sieve (100 - #10). This is adjusted for stones by multiplying it times the fraction less than 75mm (1 - (Rock 3-10 + Rock >10)/100).

Returns values for low, high, and rv: each has a single value.

	Consideration:
	1. LEP - linear extensibility  percent 
	2. Layer thickness
	3. Depth to bedrock or pan 

Logic:  Finds the thickness of each horizon for all horizons in the 0 to 85cm range.  Portions outside the depth range are not considered in the horizon thickness.  Then finds the shrink-swell value (linear extensibility  percent (LEP)) for the thickest horizon.  These two values are multiplied together and summed to provide a single value for thickness of horizon and shrink-swell.

Returns values for low, high and rv: each has a single value.

Finds the number of months in the growing season where soil moisture status is "wet" or "saturation".  The growing season is defined for MO9 as:

taxonomic temperature regime	corresponding months
----------------------------	---------------------
cryic, isofrigid or pergelic	July and August

frigid or mesic			May, June, July, 
				August, and September

thermic 			March, April, May, 
			        June, July, August,
				September, and October
				
isothermic,			Jan., Feb., March, April,
isohyperthermic,		May, June, July, August,
                 		September, October, 
				November and December

isomesic, hyperthermic	        February, March, April,
		                May, June, July, August,
                		September, October, 
				November and December
				
Returns values for low, high, and rv: each has a single value.

propname: DPTH TO BULK DENSITY DIFFERENCE >.25 BELOW AN ORGANIC
description:
Bulk density above a "normal" level of compaction limits root growth.  This property calculates a theoretical ideal bulk density for that proportion of sand, silt, clay in the horizon.  The "ideal" bulk density is then subtracted from from the given bulk density.  If the difference is greater than  a calculated threshold, the layer has a root-limiting bulk density.

Reference: Pierce, F. J., W. E. Larson, R. H. Dowdy, and W. A. P. Graham.1983. Productivity of Soils: Assessing Long-term Changes Due to Erosion. J. Soil Water Conserv. 38:39-44.

The ratio of the difference between the observed bulk density and the "optimal" or "non-limiting" bulk density and the calculated difference between a limiting bulk density and a non-limiting bulk density at each combination of s, si, and c.  This is calculated by: delta=((0.002081*sandtotal_r)+(0.003912*silttotal_r)+0.044351).


Calculation:    ((dbthirdbar_r-(((sandtotal_r*1.65)/100)+((silttotal_r*1.40)/100)+((claytotal_r*1.30)/100))) > delta)

Assumptions:	The "ideal" bulk density for a sand is about 1.65 g/cm3
		The "ideal" bulk density for a silt is about 1.40 g/cm3
		The "ideal" bulk density for a clay is about 1.30 g/cm3

Data used: claytotal from component horizon table.
	Consideration:
	1.  Clay percent

description:
dark 7/14/2005
Script as originally written assigned all unifieds to low and high. Therefore
 the low and high did not represent a range. Also, if the rv unified was gravel,
 the low and high would also always be gravel. If the rv was not gravel, the
 low and high may or may not be gravel. To overcome this oddity regarding the range, 
 I changed script to rv only (commented out the low and high; modified the rv).

Script as currently written only keeps horizons with unifieds. Therefore R, Cr,
 and *f*/mat horizons are not part of selected set. That is why it outputs data
 for the horizon above the bedrock or permafrost horizon. This works but only luck
 would have it, as opposed to keeping all horizons and then outputting data for the
 horizon above the bedrock or permafrost.
 
Added "Null not rated" hedge to rule.

propname: BULK DENSITY MAX AND 200 SIEVE > 25 IN DEPTH 0-60cm (TX)
description:
Data used:  hzdept, sieveno200, and dbthirdbar from the horizon table.
	Considerations:
	1.  Horizon depth < 60cm
	2.  Passing the sieveno200
	3.  Maximum bulk denstiy

Logic:  Finds the highest value of Bulk Density 1/3 Bar for any horizon whose RV depths intersect the range 0 to 24" (0 to 60 cm) and has more then 25% passing the 200 sieve.  A default value of 0 is assigned when passing 200 sieve is less then or equal to 25%.  In this case, data  present by the construct of the query will result in NULL data if the passing 200 sieve is less than 25% and no rating can be generated for these soils.  Therefore a default value of 0 is assigned to soil horizon that do not have null data and do not meet the conditions of the defining query.  If bulk density or passing the 200 sieve are null then not data is reported and the criteria is assigned not rated.

Returns values for low, high, and rv: each has a single value.

propname: HIGH WATER TABLE HWT Not Dry (TX)
description:
Data used: comonth.month, soimoiststat, and soimoistdept from component month and component soil moisture table.
	Consideration:
	1.  soimoiststat = "wet" or "saturation" 
	2.  Soil moisture depth
	3.  Mean Annual Precipitation MAP
	4.  Taxonomic Temperature Regime
	5.  Month

Finds the shallowest depth to soil moisture status "wet" or "saturation" for all months in the growing season where MAP is > 1100. The growing season for MO9 is defined as:

taxonomic temperature regime	corresponding months
----------------------------	---------------------
cryic, isofrigid or pergelic	July and August

frigid or mesic			May, June, July, 
				August, and September

thermic 			March, April, May, 
				June, July, August,
				September and October
				
isothermic,			January, February, March,
isohyperthermic,		April, May, June, July, August,
				August, September, October, 
				November and December

isomesic, hyperthermic	February, March, April,
				May, June, July, August,
				September, October, 
				November and December
				
Returns values for low, high, and rv: each has a single value.

propname: Ksat min above restriction l, h, rv 24 to 60 inches
description:

Finds the lowest value for permeability (K-Sat) in horizons that have any portion in the depth range 24" to 60" (60-150 cm) and above a restrictive feature.

Returns values for low, high, and rv: each has a single value.

Data used: MAP and MAAT from component horizon table.
	Consideration:
	1.  MAP
	2.  MAAT
		
Logic: Computes the ratio between mean annual precipitation and mean annual air temperature.
Example MAP/MAAT= ration precipitation to air temperature.

Returns calculated value for rv.

Data used: awc from component horizon table.
	Consideration:
	1.  AWC
	2.   DEPTH TO FIRST WATER AND ROOT RESTRICTIVE LAYER or 120cm
	3.  Layer Thickness
	
Logic: Computes the total of Available Water Capacity from a depth of 25cm (10") to the first water and root restrictive layer, or to 120cm (48"), whichever is first.  The total is computed by multiplying the horizon AWC by the horizon thickness for that portion of each horizon in the depth range, then summing across horizons.

Returns values for low, high, and rv: each has a single value.

Data used: awc from component horizon table.
	Consideration:

	2.   DEPTH TO FIRST WATER AND ROOT RESTRICTIVE LAYER or 25cm
	3.  Layer Thickness

The total is computed by multiplying the horizon AWC by the horizon thickness for that portion of each horizon in the depth range, then summing across horizons.

Returns values for low, high, and rv: each has a single value.

Data used: flodfreqcl, floddurcl, and month from the component month (comonth) table and taxtempregime from the component table.
	Consideration:
	1.  Flood Frequency class
	2.  Flood Duration class
	3.  Taxonomic Temperature Regime
	4.  Month

Logic:  Assigns a numeric values to flooding frequency and duration classes for all months in the growing season.  The numeric frequency values are multiplied by the numeric duration values to calculate the most restrictive flooding interaction during the growing season is defined for MO9 as:  

Assigned numeric values are:

Flooding Frequency Class		Flooding Duration Class
"frequent" then 0.85 			"long" then 0.95  
"very frequent" then 0.70		"very long" then 0.85
Else 1.0				Else 1.0 

Example frequent long flooding would be given a value of .085 * 0.95 = 0.808

taxonomic temperature regime	corresponding months
----------------------------	---------------------
cryic, isofrigid or pergelic	July and August

frigid or mesic			May, June, July, 
				August, and September

thermic 			March, April, May, 
				June, July, August,
				September, and October
				
isothermic,			January, February, March,
isohyperthermic,		April, May, June, July, August,
				August, September, October, 
				November and December

isomesic, hyperthermic		February, March, April,
				May, June, July, August,
				September, October, 
				November and December
				
Returns values for rv.

"occasional" then 0.95			"long" then 0.85  
"frequent" then 0.75 			"very long" then 0.75

propname: DEPTH TO ROOT LIMITING BULK DENSITY BELOW AN ORGANIC
description:
Bulk density above a "normal" level of compaction limits root growth.  This property calculates a theoretical ideal bulk density for that proportion of sand, silt, clay in the horizon.  The "ideal" bulk density is then subtracted from from the given bulk density.  If the difference is greater than  a calculated threshold, the layer has a root-limiting bulk density.

Reference: Pierce, F. J., W. E. Larson, R. H. Dowdy, and W. A. P. Graham.1983. Productivity of Soils: Assessing Long-term Changes Due to Erosion. J. Soil Water Conserv. 38:39-44.

The ratio of the difference between the observed bulk density and the "optimal" or "non-limiting" bulk density and the calculated difference between a limiting bulk density and a non-limiting bulk density at each combination of s, si, and c.  This is calculated by: delta=((0.002081*sandtotal_r)+(0.003912*silttotal_r)+0.044351).


Calculation:    ((dbthirdbar_r-(((sandtotal_r*1.65)/100)+((silttotal_r*1.40)/100)+((claytotal_r*1.30)/100))) > delta)

Assumptions:	The "ideal" bulk density for a sand is about 1.65 g/cm3
		The "ideal" bulk density for a silt is about 1.40 g/cm3
		The "ideal" bulk density for a clay is about 1.30 g/cm3

propname: DRY SOIL MONTHS - PROPORTION OF GROWING SEASON
description:
Finds the of months for a component that do not have wet soil moisture status.


exec sql select comonth.month
from component, comonth
where join component to comonth
and not exists(select * from cosoilmoist where soimoiststat = "wet" and join cosoilmoist to comonth
and (taxtempcl in ("hypergelic", "pergelic", "subgelic") 
and comonth.month in ("jul", "aug"))

and comonth.month in ("feb", "mar", "apr", "may", "jun", "jul", "aug", "sep", "oct"))

or (taxtempregime in ("mesic")
and comonth.month in ("mar", "apr", "may", "jun", "jul", "aug", "sep", "oct"))

or (taxtempregime in ("cryic")
and comonth.month in ("jun", "jul", "aug"))

or (taxtempregime in ("hyperthermic")

sort by comonth.month.

Data used: slopelenusle and slope from component table.
	Consideration:
	1. Slope
	2. Slope length
		
Finds the "Slope-Length of Slope" index value from the following equation:
((0.065 + (0.0456 * slope_r) + (0.006541*(slope_r ** 2)))*((slopelenusle_r/22.1) ** mexp_r))

Where mexp_r is the slope exponent from the following list.
slope_r <1 then mexp_r = 0.2223
slope_r => 1 and <2 then mexp_r = 0.2684
slope_r => 2 and <3 then mexp_r = 0.3348
slope_r => 3 and <4 then mexp_r = 0.4001
slope_r => 4 and <5 then mexp_r = 0.4465
slope_r => 5 and <6 then mexp_r = 0.4732
slope_r => 6 and <7 then mexp_r = 0.4869
slope_r => 7 and <8 then mexp_r = 0.4936
slope_r => 8 and <9 then mexp_r = 0.4969
slope_r => 9 and <10 then mexp_r = 0.4985
slope_r => 10 then mexp_r= 0.5

Returns calculation values as rv.

propname: CLS Lateral - Horizon Texture Groups old (LEP<6)
description:
Calls the property "CLS Lateral - Rock Fragments" and pulls the sand, silt, and clay percentages and the LEP for each horizon to find the texture of each horizon and classify each horizon into texture groups based on the Missouri Department of Health code for governing on-site sewage systems.  Horizons with no sand, silt, or clay size fractions (e.g. R or Cr) are not rated.
These texture groups are as follows:

Group 1:  Sand and Loamy Sand
Group 2:  Sandy Loam
Group 3:  Silt Loam, Silt, Sandy Clay Loam, Clay Loam (with <35% clay), and Silty Clay Loam (with <35% clay)
Group 4a: Sandy Clay, Silty Clay, and Clay, each must have LEP <= 6
Group 4b: Sandy Clay, Silty Clay, Clay, Clay Loam (with >=35% clay), and Silty Clay Loam (with >=35% clay)
Group 5:  Any texture with >50% rocks

description:
Data used:  hzdept_r, sieveno10_l, sieveno10_h, and sieveno10_r from  the component and component horizon.
	Considerations:
	1.  Percent Passing the 10# sieve and
	2.  Percent coarse fragments > 3 inches.

Logic:  Finds the layer with the maximum rock fragments of size 2mm to <75mm  in soil surface.  

The 2mm to <75mm fragments are represented by the percent retained on the #10 sieve (100 - #10). This is adjusted for stones by multiplying it times the fraction less than 75mm (1 - (Rock 3-10 + Rock >10)/100).

Returns values for low, high, and rv: each has a single value.

Finds the maximum aluminum value for the component.
 
Returns max values for low,rv,high value.

Some agricultural crops suffer from aluminum toxicity when the Al saturation is only 10%. Aluminum interferes with the photosynthetic cycle by complexing with phosphate, so with high soluble aluminum the plant is starved for phosphate. Al-toxicity also stunts root growth thereby limiting the amount of soil the plant can exploit for nutrients. Stunted roots can also limit water uptake and can cause plants to wilt with only a few days without water. Some plants (e.g. cassava) have high tolerance to high levels of soluble aluminum. High soluble Al and acidity may adversely affect soil health by inhibiting beneficial organisms. When liming soils with high soluble aluminum the rule of thumb is to add 1.5 tons of CaCO3 per acre for every milliequivalents of soluble aluminum. The pH only needs to be raised to about 5.5 to eliminate the harmful effects of high soluble aluminum. (Source: Dr. Robert Gavenda, PhD; PowerPoint presentation on soil degradation)

About one-third of the tropics (1.5 billion hectares) has sufficiently strong soil acidity for soluble aluminum to be toxic to most crop species. This constraint is defined as having more than 60% Al saturation in some part of the top 50 cm of soil. A soil pH value of less than 5.5 usually indicates this problem (Evans and Kamprath, 1970). Aluminum toxicity is most prevalent in the humid tropics and acid savannas. This constraint is found mainly in soils classified as oxisols, ultisols and closely related inceptisols and is correlated with low nutrient capital reserves. Aluminum toxicity is usually the overwhelming constraint in these soils and must be tackled first, either by modern lime application practices, by using Al-tolerant plant species or by breeding for Al-tolerant varieties (Sanchez and Salinas, 1981). It is relevant to note that aluminum toxicity is rare in most smallholder farming areas of subhumid and semiarid Africa, except for parts of Rwanda, Burundi, Northern Zambia, Southern Congo, KwaZulu Natal Province in South Africa and in some sandy soils of Zimbabwe (Sanchez et al., 1997). Two-thirds of the tropics does not have enough aluminum saturation to worry about. Aluminum toxicity can become a positive soil quality attribute when using Al-tolerant plants in P-deficient soils. The low pH facilitates the dissolution of phosphate rocks, letting, in effect, the H+ ions in the soil do what a superphosphate factory doestreating rock phosphates with acids (Sanchez and Salinas, 1981). High aluminum saturation, as defined by this modifier, is also a positive attribute for rubber and tea production (Smith, 1989).  (Source: Fertility capability soil classification: a tool to help assess soil quality in the tropics by Pedro A. Sancheza,, Cheryl A. Palma, and Stanley W. Buol)

propname: DEPTH TO HIGH BULK DENSITY BELOW AN ORGANIC LAYER
description:
Bulk density above a "normal" level of compaction limits root growth.  This property calculates a theoretical ideal bulk density for that proportion of sand, silt, clay in the horizon.  The "ideal" bulk density is then subtracted from from the given bulk density.  If the difference is greater than  a calculated threshold, the layer has a root-limiting bulk density.

Reference: Pierce, F. J., W. E. Larson, R. H. Dowdy, and W. A. P. Graham.1983. Productivity of Soils: Assessing Long-term Changes Due to Erosion. J. Soil Water Conserv. 38:39-44.

The ratio of the difference between the observed bulk density and the "optimal" or "non-limiting" bulk density and the calculated difference between a limiting bulk density and a non-limiting bulk density at each combination of s, si, and c.  This is calculated by: delta=((0.002081*sandtotal_r)+(0.003912*silttotal_r)+0.044351).


Calculation:    ((dbthirdbar_r-(((sandtotal_r*1.65)/100)+((silttotal_r*1.40)/100)+((claytotal_r*1.30)/100))) > delta)

Assumptions:	The "ideal" bulk density for a sand is about 1.65 g/cm3
		The "ideal" bulk density for a silt is about 1.40 g/cm3
		The "ideal" bulk density for a clay is about 1.30 g/cm3

propname: DEPTH TO LIMITING BULK DENSITY DIFFERENCE BELOW AN ORGANIC
description:
Bulk density above a "normal" level of compaction limits root growth.  This property calculates a theoretical ideal bulk density for that proportion of sand, silt, clay in the horizon.  The "ideal" bulk density is then subtracted from from the given bulk density.  If the difference is greater than  a calculated threshold, the layer has a root-limiting bulk density.

Reference: Pierce, F. J., W. E. Larson, R. H. Dowdy, and W. A. P. Graham.1983. Productivity of Soils: Assessing Long-term Changes Due to Erosion. J. Soil Water Conserv. 38:39-44.

The ratio of the difference between the observed bulk density and the "optimal" or "non-limiting" bulk density and the calculated difference between a limiting bulk density and a non-limiting bulk density at each combination of s, si, and c.  This is calculated by: delta=((0.002081*sandtotal_r)+(0.003912*silttotal_r)+0.044351).


Calculation:    ((dbthirdbar_r-(((sandtotal_r*1.65)/100)+((silttotal_r*1.40)/100)+((claytotal_r*1.30)/100))) > delta)

Assumptions:	The "ideal" bulk density for a sand is about 1.65 g/cm3
		The "ideal" bulk density for a silt is about 1.40 g/cm3
		The "ideal" bulk density for a clay is about 1.30 g/cm3

Data used: hzdept_r, hzdepb_r, unifiedcl, rvindicator from  component, component horizon, and component horizon unified tables.
	Considerations:
	1.  Calculated horizon thickness;
	2.  Horizon depth;

Logic:  Finds the first or rv Unified class of the thickest soil horizons between 25 and 180cm where the Unified class rv is set to yes else the first Unified class listed is selected.  The representative or first Unified class for the thickest horizon is returned as the rv value.

Portions outside the depth range are not considered in the horizon thickness.

#assign unifiedcl	isnull(gypsum_r) then unifiedcl else if gypsum_r >= 40 then "sm" else unifiedcl.


define layer_thickness  hzdepb_r - hzdept_r.

define rv  hzdepb_r - hzdept_r.

define unithick		regroup layer_thickness by unifiedcl aggregate sum.

# Determine the maximum horizon thickness in the range.

define maximum_thickness arraymax(unithick).

define max_thickness maximum_thickness > 0 ? maximum_thickness : 1/0.

# Find the unified class for the thickest group of layers.
 define rvm   lookup(max_thickness, unithick, unifiedcl).

Data used:  hzdept_r, sandvf_r , silttotal_r, claytotal_r from the component horizon tables.
	Consideration:
	1. percent very fine sand, silt, and clay of the surface layer

Logic: Perdicts PM2.5 index. The index estimates a potential for the soil to be a source of PM2.5 particulate materials.  Where:  Average of sand and clay regression where PM2.5 index = 2.000 - 0.014 * sandtotal_r and PM2.5 index = 0.711 + 0.022 * claytotal_r are averaged to give a smooth index based on both sand and clay particle size 

Returns values for rv: each component has a single value.

Reference:  Carvacho, 2003; Measurement of PM2.5 emission potential from soil using the UC Davis resuspension test chamber.

Data used:  hzdept_r, hzdepb_r, lep_l, lep_h, lep_r from the component and component horizon tables.
	Consideration:
	1. LEP - linear extensibility  percent 
	2. Layer thickness
	3. Depth to bedrock or pan 

Logic:  Finds the thickness of each horizon for all horizons in the 50 to 180cm range.  Portions outside the depth range are not considered in the horizon thickness.  Then finds the shrink-swell value (linear extensibility  percent (LEP)) for the thickest horizon. # Find the weighted average soilph in the depth 0-100cm.



define rv     	wtavg((if hzdepb_r - o_thickness <=100 THEN default ELSE lookup(1, in_range, soilph)), layer_thickness).

Data used: claytotal from component horizon table.
	Consideration:
	1.  Clay percent
	
Logic: Finds the maximum clay percent for any horizon in the depths 80 to 160 cm.  Portions outside the depth range are not considered in the horizon thickness.
 
Returns values for low, high, and rv: normally each has a single value.

Data used:  hzdept_r, sieveno10_l, sieveno10_h, sieveno10_r, frag3to10_l, frag3to10_h, frag3to10_r, fraggt10_l, fraggt10_h and fraggt10_r from  the component, component horizon, and component restrictions tables.
	Considerations:
	2.  Horizon depth;
	3.  Percent Passing the 10# sieve and
	4.  Percent coarse fragments > 3 inches.

Logic:  Finds the layer with the maximum gravel content of size 2mm to < 75mm  within a depth of 80 to 160cm.  Uses sieve and rock percents from the Horizon table.

The 2mm to <75mm fragments are represented by the percent retained on the #10 sieve (100 - #10). This is adjusted for rock fragments by multiplying it times the fraction less than 75mm (1 - (Rock 3-10 + Rock >10)/100).

Returns values for low, high, and rv: each has a single value.

propname: MONTHS WATER TABLE BELOW 120CM DURING GROWING SEASON - COUNT
description:
Finds the of months for a component that do not have wet soil moisture status.


exec sql select comonth.month
from component, comonth
where join component to comonth
and not exists(select * from cosoilmoist where soimoiststat = "wet" and join cosoilmoist to comonth
and (taxtempcl in ("hypergelic", "pergelic", "subgelic") 
and comonth.month in ("jul", "aug"))

or (taxtempregime in ("thermic")
and comonth.month in ("feb", "mar", "apr", "may", "jun", "jul", "aug", "sep", "oct"))

or (taxtempregime in ("mesic")
and comonth.month in ("mar", "apr", "may", "jun", "jul", "aug", "sep", "oct"))

or (taxtempregime in ("cryic")
and comonth.month in ("jun", "jul", "aug"))

or (taxtempregime in ("frigid", "isofrigid") 
and comonth.month in ("may", "jun", "jul", "aug", "sep")) 

or (taxtempregime in ("hyperthermic") 
and comonth.month in ("feb", "mar", "apr", "may", "jun", "jul", "aug", "sep", "oct", "nov", "dec")) 

or (taxtempregime in ("isothermic", "isohyperthermic", "isomesic") 
and comonth.month in ("jan", "feb", "mar", "apr", "may", "jun", "jul", "aug", "sep", "oct", "nov", "dec")));
sort by comonth.month.

derive growth from rv using "NSSC Data":"GROWING SEASON NUMBER OF MONTHS".

# Label month code with month name.

define dry	ARRAYCOUNT(comonth.month).

define rv	dry/growth.

Calculates the Mean Annual Precipitation minus the potential evapotranspiration using an equation as close to Hamon (1963) as was possible.  Result is mm per year.  Can be negative in dry climates.  A single value for thr rv is returned.

Reference: Hamon, W. R., 1963. Computation of direct runoff amounts from storm rainfall.  Int Assoc. Sci. Hydrol. Pub 63:52-62.

Calculates Kf and Kw.

Data elements used in the K factor calculation:
     - Structure type
     - Structure size
     - clay (rv)
     - silt (rv)
     - very fine sand (rv)
     - organic matter (rv)
     - Ksat (rv)
     - rock fragment volume (rv), Horizon Fragment Table 
     - rock fragment hardness, Horizon Fragment Table
     
1. The calculation is based on the nomograph in NSSH Exhibit 618-12 and Ag Hndk no. 537. The nomograph does not apply to soils of volcanic origin, organic soils, Oxisols or low activity clay soils, calcareous soil, high gypsum soils, and soils high in mica. Also, the nomograph is less accurate for subsoils than for surface soils.
2. Minimum Ksat is based on the minimum Ksat within the top 50 cm from the top of the horizon being rated for K; includes bedrock.
3. If a horizon classifies as organic (based on criteria in Soil Taxonomy) then a NULL is returned.
4. When structure type and size are NULL then blocky, platy or massive (class 4) is assumed.
5. When organic matter is > 4% in mineral horizons, 4% is used in the calculation.
6. If organic matter, silt, or very fine sand are not populated, a NULL is returned.
7. Ksat for each horizon in the profile must be populated, otherwise minimum Ksat will not be accurately estimated.
8. Kw is adjusted when rock fragments are greater than or equal to 15% by volume.

This is Cathy Seybold's calculation, modified into a property script.

propname: WATER TABLE W/IN 100CM MONTHS DURING GROWING SEASON - COUNT
description:
Finds the of months for a component that do not have wet soil moisture status.


exec sql select comonth.month
from component, comonth
where join component to comonth
and not exists(select * from cosoilmoist where soimoiststat = "wet" and join cosoilmoist to comonth
and (taxtempcl in ("hypergelic", "pergelic", "subgelic") 
and comonth.month in ("jul", "aug"))

or (taxtempregime in ("thermic")
and comonth.month in ("feb", "mar", "apr", "may", "jun", "jul", "aug", "sep", "oct"))

or (taxtempregime in ("mesic")
and comonth.month in ("mar", "apr", "may", "jun", "jul", "aug", "sep", "oct"))

or (taxtempregime in ("cryic")
and comonth.month in ("jun", "jul", "aug"))

or (taxtempregime in ("frigid", "isofrigid") 
and comonth.month in ("may", "jun", "jul", "aug", "sep")) 

or (taxtempregime in ("hyperthermic") 
and comonth.month in ("feb", "mar", "apr", "may", "jun", "jul", "aug", "sep", "oct", "nov", "dec")) 

or (taxtempregime in ("isothermic", "isohyperthermic", "isomesic") 
and comonth.month in ("jan", "feb", "mar", "apr", "may", "jun", "jul", "aug", "sep", "oct", "nov", "dec")));
sort by comonth.month.

derive growth from rv using "NSSC Data":"GROWING SEASON NUMBER OF MONTHS".

# Label month code with month name.

define dry	ARRAYCOUNT(comonth.month).

define rv	dry/growth.

Data used: fraggt10, frag3to10, and sieveno10 from component horizon table.
	Consideration:
	1.  Percent passing the # 10 sieve.
	2.  Fragments 3 to 10 inch in diameter.
	3.  Fragments greater then 10 inch in diameter.
	
Logic: Computes the percentage of coarse fragments in the surface horizon (top depth = 0) greater then 2mm in diameter.
The 2mm to 3" fragments are represented by the percent retained on the #10 sieve (100 - #10). This is adjusted for stones by multiplying it times the fraction less than 3" (1 - (Rock 3-10 + Rock >10)/100).  Then the percentages for rocks 3" to 10", and rocks > 10", are added on to determine the total fragments > 2mm.

Returns values for low, high, and rv: each has a single value.

propname: GRL-RPI-DPTH TO BULK DENSITY DIFFERENCE >.25 BELOW AN ORGANI
description:
Copied from DPTH TO BULK DENSITY DIFFERENCE >.25 BELOW AN ORGANIC; NSSC Data; Interps Holding.

Bulk density above a "normal" level of compaction limits root growth.  This property calculates a theoretical ideal bulk density for that proportion of sand, silt, clay in the horizon.  The "ideal" bulk density is then subtracted from from the given bulk density.  If the difference is greater than  a calculated threshold, the layer has a root-limiting bulk density.

Reference: Pierce, F. J., W. E. Larson, R. H. Dowdy, and W. A. P. Graham.1983. Productivity of Soils: Assessing Long-term Changes Due to Erosion. J. Soil Water Conserv. 38:39-44.

The ratio of the difference between the observed bulk density and the "optimal" or "non-limiting" bulk density and the calculated difference between a limiting bulk density and a non-limiting bulk density at each combination of s, si, and c.  This is calculated by: delta=((0.002081*sandtotal_r)+(0.003912*silttotal_r)+0.044351).


Calculation:    ((dbthirdbar_r-(((sandtotal_r*1.65)/100)+((silttotal_r*1.40)/100)+((claytotal_r*1.30)/100))) > delta)

Assumptions:	The "ideal" bulk density for a sand is about 1.65 g/cm3
		The "ideal" bulk density for a silt is about 1.40 g/cm3
		The "ideal" bulk density for a clay is about 1.30 g/cm3

This script looks for the phrase *limeston*residuum* to return any soil that may be residual over limestone.  Also, the taxonomic great group is examined for the "Pale" feature.  The map unit name and local phase are examined for "karst".  A numeric rating is returned for various combinations of these, as shown below:


If the parent material is limestone residuum and the soil is in a "Pale" great group, then the rating is .1.

If the parent material is limestone residuum and the soil is in a "Pale" great group and either the map unit name or the local phase indicates "karst", then the rating is .4.

If the parent material is limestone residuum then the rating is .5.

If the parent material is limestone residuum and  either the map unit name or the local phase indicates "karst", then the rating is .8.

Some agricultural crops suffer from aluminum toxicity when the Al saturation is only 10%. Aluminum interferes with the photosynthetic cycle by complexing with phosphate, so with high soluble aluminum the plant is starved for phosphate. Al-toxicity also stunts root growth thereby limiting the amount of soil the plant can exploit for nutrients. Stunted roots can also limit water uptake and can cause plants to wilt with only a few days without water. Some plants (e.g. cassava) have high tolerance to high levels of soluble aluminum. High soluble Al and acidity may adversely affect soil health by inhibiting beneficial organisms. When liming soils with high soluble aluminum the rule of thumb is to add 1.5 tons of CaCO3 per acre for every milliequivalents of soluble aluminum. The pH only needs to be raised to about 5.5 to eliminate the harmful effects of high soluble aluminum. (Source: Dr. Robert Gavenda, PhD; PowerPoint presentation on soil degradation)

About one-third of the tropics (1.5 billion hectares) has sufficiently strong soil acidity for soluble aluminum to be toxic to most crop species. This constraint is defined as having more than 60% Al saturation in some part of the top 50 cm of soil. A soil pH value of less than 5.5 usually indicates this problem (Evans and Kamprath, 1970). Aluminum toxicity is most prevalent in the humid tropics and acid savannas. This constraint is found mainly in soils classified as oxisols, ultisols and closely related inceptisols and is correlated with low nutrient capital reserves. Aluminum toxicity is usually the overwhelming constraint in these soils and must be tackled first, either by modern lime application practices, by using Al-tolerant plant species or by breeding for Al-tolerant varieties (Sanchez and Salinas, 1981). It is relevant to note that aluminum toxicity is rare in most smallholder farming areas of subhumid and semiarid Africa, except for parts of Rwanda, Burundi, Northern Zambia, Southern Congo, KwaZulu Natal Province in South Africa and in some sandy soils of Zimbabwe (Sanchez et al., 1997). Two-thirds of the tropics does not have enough aluminum saturation to worry about. Aluminum toxicity can become a positive soil quality attribute when using Al-tolerant plants in P-deficient soils. The low pH facilitates the dissolution of phosphate rocks, letting, in effect, the H+ ions in the soil do what a superphosphate factory doestreating rock phosphates with acids (Sanchez and Salinas, 1981). High aluminum saturation, as defined by this modifier, is also a positive attribute for rubber and tea production (Smith, 1989).  (Source: Fertility capability soil classification: a tool to help assess soil quality in the tropics by Pedro A. Sancheza,, Cheryl A. Palma, and Stanley W. Buol)

propname: oldSoil OC (kg/m2) to 2 m or bedrock/duripan or petro* (NPS)
description:
Evaluates soil organic carbon (SOC) to a depth of two meters or to the occurrence of any type of bedrock or other certain types of restrictive layers. 

rev. SBSouthard 10/09
SBSouthard 3/2009

1. Soil organic carbon result is in kg/m2 to the depth of the soil.  Conversion to pounds/acre: (kg/m) X (2.2 lbs/kg) X (4047 m2/acre); so, kg/m X 8903 = pounds SOC/acre. Likewise, kg/m2 * 4.4515 = tons/acre.

2. This rule evaluates to 2 meter depth or to representative top depth of any bedrock kind, any petro horizon and any duripan. Other types of restrictions were not coded into the depth to restriction subproperty used in the main interpretation property script because the concern is not rooting depth restrictions but total amount of SOC stabilized in soils on a volumetric basis. It was decided to include stabilized soil organic carbon that may exist below a strongly contrasted particle size. In a Fluvent, for example, or buried old surfaces below tephra deposits there may be large stores of carbon that lie below other kinds of restrictive layers.

3. The calculation reports on a volumetric whole soil basis, corrected for representative rock fragments in database. The representative amount of soil passing the #10 sieve, rock fragment particle density, and the representative 1/3 bar density of the soil is given priority. If sieves and RF weights are NULL the rock fragment volume table is used instead. The soil organic carbon is converted from horizon soil organic matter content stored as a weight percent of the < 2mm fraction of the soil and recalculated on a whole soil basis. If soil organic matter in the database is NULL, SOC is assumed to be zero.

4. The NPS SOC class rule attached to this property was designed using an arbitrary linear curve in the associated evaluation. The curve was designed so that the "fuzzy value" multiplied by 1000 gives you that actual amount SOC calculated for the component in the NASIS data. Units are kg/meter2 to some depth when multiplied by 1000 for the rule.

Data issues:

1. NULL 1/3 bulk density may exist for mineral horizons and this calculation will assign a bulk density value of 0.2 because in most cases NULL 1/3 bulk density in the data occurs with O horizons. Using this assumption, in some cases the amount of SOC will be underestimated for non-organic horizons with no bulk density populated.

2. Particle densities vary over the country but 2.65 was used universally. More complex default queries could be written using parent material. It is not apparent if map results with broad SOC classes would reflect the extra effort to refine particle densities. This will result in either overestimation or underestimation of SOC depending on rock type. The property script can be copied and edited for particle densities for individual areas.

3. An alternative subproperty script was added in October 2009 to use the horizon rock fragment volume table instead of sieves if sieves, RF 3-10" and >10" data columns are NULL.

propname: SOC (kg/m2) to 2 m bedrock/duripan or petro* (NPS)
description:
Evaluates soil organic carbon (SOC) to a depth of two meters or to the occurrence of any type of bedrock or other certain types of restrictive layers. 


rev. SBSouthard 10/09
SBSouthard 3/2009

1. Soil organic carbon result is in kg/m2 to the depth of the soil.  Conversion to pounds/acre: (kg/m) X (2.2 lbs/kg) X (4047 m2/acre); so, kg/m X 8903 = pounds SOC/acre. Likewise, kg/m2 * 4.4515 = tons/acre.

2. This rule evaluates to 2 meter depth or to representative top depth of any bedrock kind, any petro horizon and any duripan. Other types of restrictions were not coded into the depth to restriction subproperty used in the main interpretation property script because the concern is not rooting depth restrictions but total amount of SOC stabilized in soils on a volumetric basis. It was decided to include stabilized soil organic carbon that may exist below a strongly contrasted particle size. In a Fluvent, for example, or buried old surfaces below tephra deposits there may be large stores of carbon that lie below other kinds of restrictive layers.

3. The calculation reports on a volumetric whole soil basis, corrected for representative rock fragments in database. The representative amount of soil passing the #10 sieve, rock fragment particle density, and the representative 1/3 bar density of the soil is given priority. If sieves and RF weights are NULL the rock fragment volume table is used instead. The soil organic carbon is converted from horizon soil organic matter content stored as a weight percent of the < 2mm fraction of the soil and recalculated on a whole soil basis. If soil organic matter in the database is NULL, SOC is assumed to be zero.

4. The NPS SOC class rule attached to this property was designed using an arbitrary linear curve in the associated evaluation. The curve was designed so that the "fuzzy value" multiplied by 1000 gives you that actual amount SOC calculated for the component in the NASIS data. Units are kg/meter2 to some depth when multiplied by 1000 for the rule.

Data issues:

1. NULL 1/3 bulk density may exist for mineral horizons and this calculation will assign a bulk density value of 0.2 because in most cases NULL 1/3 bulk density in the data occurs with O horizons. Using this assumption, in some cases the amount of SOC will be underestimated for non-organic horizons with no bulk density populated.

2. Particle densities vary over the country but 2.65 was used universally. More complex default queries could be written using parent material. It is not apparent if map results with broad SOC classes would reflect the extra effort to refine particle densities. This will result in either overestimation or underestimation of SOC depending on rock type. The property script can be copied and edited for particle densities for individual areas.

3. An alternative subproperty script was added in October 2009 to use the horizon rock fragment volume table instead of sieves if sieves, RF 3-10" and >10" data columns are NULL.

rev. SBSouthard 10/09
SBSouthard 3/2009

1. Soil inorganic carbon (SIC) result is in kg/m2 to the depth of the soil.  Conversion to pounds/acre: (kg/m) X (2.2 lbs/kg) X (4047 m2/acre); so, kg/m X 8903 = pounds SIC/acre. Likewise, kg/m2 * 4.4515 = tons/acre.

2. This property evaluates to 2 meter depth or to representative top depth of any bedrock kind. Other types of restrictions were not coded into the depth to restriction subproperty used in the main interpretation property script because the concern is not rooting depth restrictions but total amount of SIC stabilized in soils on a volumetric basis. It was decided to include stabilized soil inorganic carbon that may exist below a strongly contrasted particle size or sequential duripans or horizons that may have carbonate data below cemented horizons such as petrocalcic horizons. The property does not take into consideration carbonate coatings and pendants on rocks or pans, or the carbonates contained within cemented horizons that may not be represented in the attribute data (but are by definition part of the series control section). The curve was designed so that the "fuzzy value" multiplied by 1000 gives you that actual amount SIC calculated for the component in the NASIS data. Units are kg/meter2 to some depth when multiplied by 1000 for the rule.

Using this assumption, in some cases the amount of SIC will be underestimated for non-organic horizons with no bulk density populated.

2. Particle densities vary over the country but 2.65 was used universally. More complex default queries could be written using parent material. It is not apparent if map results with broad SIC classes would reflect the extra effort to refine particle densities. This will result in either overestimation or underestimation of SIC depending on rock type. The property script can be copied and edited for particle densities for individual areas.

3. An addition subproperty script was added in October 2009 to use the horizon rock fragment volume table instead of sieves if sieves, RF 3-10" and >10" data columns are NULL.

Retrieves the weighted average n-value from the mineral surface to 100cm or to a restriction, whichever is first. Any thin organic layer present at the surface is removed.  The  weighted average n-value is for that portion of each horizon in the depth range.  The n-value is from Pons and Zonneveld (1965). They recognized that the cohesiveness of the soil material is related to the content of water, silt, and clay, as influenced the clay mineralogy.  The materials they dealt with were predominantly illitic and they recognized that kaolinitic or montmorillinitic clays would behave differently.  

"The n-values were calculated for several hundred soil samples of mineral soils with the following formula derived from:

n = (A-0.2 R) / (L + bH)                 

Here a b-factor of 3 is used for soils with an organic matter content which has been well humified (this can be confirmed microscopically) and a b-factor of 4 for soil
samples with clearly visible plant remnants containing cell structures, etc. (cf the Appendix)...  Most Western European clays mainly consist of illite with a cation exchange capacity of about 60 m.e.p. 100 g clay."

A = the total water content compared to 100 g of dry soil
L = the clay content (lutum)
H = the organic matter content
R = the non-colloidal mineral part of the soil (mainly silt, sand and lime, R = 100-H-L)
b = the ratio of the water-adsorbtion capacity of organic matter to (illite-) clay

Translating into NASIS:
L = the clay content (lutum) = claytotal_r
H = the organic matter content = om_r
R = the non-colloidal mineral part of the soil (mainly silt, sand and lime, R = 100-H-L) = silttotal_r+sandtotal_r
b = the ratio of the water-adsorbtion capacity of organic matter to (illite-) clay = 0.3
A = the total water content compared to 100 g of dry soil = 2*wsatiated_r  (Satiated water as measured on subareal soils is not wet enough for subaqueous soils, so a multiplier of 2 is employed)

The "b" variable depends on mineralogy and could be adjusted to reflect the component data.

Thus, for a layer:

n-value=(((2*wsatiated_r)-sandtotal_r)-(0.2*(silttotal_r+sandtotal_r)))/(claytotal_r+(3*om_r)  


Pons, L.J., and I.S. Zonneveld. 1965. Soil ripening and soil classification: Initial soil formation in alluvial deposits and a classification of the resulting soils. Publ. 13. Int. Inst. Land Reclamation and Improvement, Wageningen, The Netherlands.

Returns values for low, high, and rv: each has a single value.

Evaluates soil inorganic carbon (SIC) in the upper 5 cm of the soil. SIC is inferred from the weight of CaC03 in the soil, C being 12% of the mass.
 
rev. SBSouthard 10/09
SBSouthard 3/2009

1. Soil inorganic carbon (SIC) result is in kg/m2 to the depth of the soil.  Conversion to pounds/acre: (kg/m) X (2.2 lbs/kg) X (4047 m2/acre); so, kg/m X 8903 = pounds SIC/acre. Likewise, kg/m2 * 4.4515 = tons/acre.

2. This property evaluates to 5cm depth or to representative top depth of any bedrock kind. Other types of restrictions were not coded into the depth to restriction subproperty used in the main interpretation property script because the concern is not rooting depth restrictions but total amount of SIC stabilized in soils on a volumetric basis. It was decided to include stabilized soil inorganic carbon that may exist below a strongly contrasted particle size or sequential duripans or horizons that may have carbonate data below cemented horizons such as petrocalcic horizons. The property does not take into consideration carbonate coatings and pendants on rocks or pans, or the carbonates contained within cemented horizons that may not be represented in the attribute data (but are by definition part of the series control section). These C sources may not have been considered in the CaC03 percent by weight value in the database.

3. The calculation reports on a volumetric whole soil basis, corrected for representative rock fragments in database. The representative amount of soil passing the #10 sieve, rock fragment particle density, and the representative 1/3 bar density of the soil is given priority. If sieves and RF weights are NULL the rock fragment volume table is used instead. The soil inorganic carbon is converted from horizon CaC03 content stored as a weight percent of the < 2mm fraction of the soil and recalculated on a whole soil basis. Carbon is 12% of CaC03. If soil CaC03 in the database is NULL, CaC03 is assumed to be zero.

4. The NPS SIC class rule attached to this property was designed using an arbitrary linear curve in the associated evaluation. The curve was designed so that the "fuzzy value" multiplied by 1000 gives you that actual amount SIC calculated for the component in the NASIS data. Units are kg/meter2 to some depth when multiplied by 1000 for the rule.

Data issues:

1. NULL 1/3 bulk density may exist for mineral horizons and this calculation will assign a bulk density value of 0.2 because in most cases NULL 1/3 bulk density in the data occurs with O horizons. Using this assumption, in some cases the amount of SIC will be underestimated for non-organic horizons with no bulk density populated.

2. Particle densities vary over the country but 2.65 was used universally. More complex default queries could be written using parent material. It is not apparent if map results with broad SIC classes would reflect the extra effort to refine particle densities. This will result in either overestimation or underestimation of SIC depending on rock type. The property script can be copied and edited for particle densities for individual areas.

3. An addition subproperty script was added in October 2009 to use the horizon rock fragment volume table instead of sieves if sieves, RF 3-10" and >10" data columns are NULL.

1. Soil inorganic carbon (SIC) result is in kg/m2 to the depth of the soil.  Conversion to pounds/acre: (kg/m) X (2.2 lbs/kg) X (4047 m2/acre); so, kg/m X 8903 = pounds SIC/acre. Likewise, kg/m2 * 4.4515 = tons/acre.

2. This property evaluates to 5cm depth or to representative top depth of any bedrock kind. Other types of restrictions were not coded into the depth to restriction subproperty used in the main interpretation property script because the concern is not rooting depth restrictions but total amount of SIC stabilized in soils on a volumetric basis. It was decided to include stabilized soil inorganic carbon that may exist below a strongly contrasted particle size or sequential duripans or horizons that may have carbonate data below cemented horizons such as petrocalcic horizons. The property does not take into consideration carbonate coatings and pendants on rocks or pans, or the carbonates contained within cemented horizons that may not be represented in the attribute data (but are by definition part of the series control section). These C sources may not have been considered in the CaC03 percent by weight value in the database.

3. The calculation reports on a volumetric whole soil basis, corrected for representative rock fragments in database. The representative amount of soil passing the #10 sieve, rock fragment particle density, and the representative 1/3 bar density of the soil is given priority. If sieves and RF weights are NULL the rock fragment volume table is used instead. The soil inorganic carbon is converted from horizon CaC03 content stored as a weight percent of the < 2mm fraction of the soil and recalculated on a whole soil basis. Carbon is 12% of CaC03. If soil CaC03 in the database is NULL, CaC03 is assumed to be zero.

4. The NPS SIC class rule attached to this property was designed using an arbitrary linear curve in the associated evaluation. The curve was designed so that the "fuzzy value" multiplied by 1000 gives you that actual amount SIC calculated for the component in the NASIS data. Units are kg/meter2 to some depth when multiplied by 1000 for the rule.

Data issues:

1. NULL 1/3 bulk density may exist for mineral horizons and this calculation will assign a bulk density value of 0.2 because in most cases NULL 1/3 bulk density in the data occurs with O horizons. Using this assumption, in some cases the amount of SIC will be underestimated for non-organic horizons with no bulk density populated.

2. Particle densities vary over the country but 2.65 was used universally. More complex default queries could be written using parent material. It is not apparent if map results with broad SIC classes would reflect the extra effort to refine particle densities. This will result in either overestimation or underestimation of SIC depending on rock type. The property script can be copied and edited for particle densities for individual areas.

3. An addition subproperty script was added in October 2009 to use the horizon rock fragment volume table instead of sieves if sieves, RF 3-10" and >10" data columns are NULL.

Retrieves the depth to an n-value less than 0.7 from the mineral surface to 100cm or to a restriction, whichever is first. Any thin organic layer present at the surface is removed.  The  depth to the n-value is for that portion of each horizon in the depth range.  The n-value is from Pons and Zonneveld (1965). They recognized that the cohesiveness of the soil material is related to the content of water, silt, and clay, as influenced the clay mineralogy.  The materials they dealt with were predominantly illitic and the recognized that kaolinitic or montmorillinitic clays would behave differently.  

"The n-values were calculated for several hundred soil samples of mineral soils with the following formula derived from:

n = (A-0.2 R) / (L + bH)                 

Here a b-factor of 3 is used for soils with an organic matter content which has been well humified (this can be confirmed microscopically) and a b-factor of 4 for soil
samples with clearly visible plant remnants containing cell structures, etc. (cf the Appendix)...  Most Western European clays mainly consist of illite with a cation exchange capacity of about 60 m.e.p. 100 g clay."

A = the total water content compared to 100 g of dry soil
L = the clay content (lutum)
H = the organic matter content
R = the non-colloidal mineral part of the soil (mainly silt, sand and lime, R = 100-H-L)
b = the ratio of the water-adsorbtion capacity of organic matter to (illite-) clay

Translating into NASIS:
L = the clay content (lutum) = claytotal_r
H = the organic matter content = om_r
R = the non-colloidal mineral part of the soil (mainly silt, sand and lime, R = 100-H-L) = silttotal_r+sandtotal_r
b = the ratio of the water-adsorbtion capacity of organic matter to (illite-) clay = 0.3
A = the total water content compared to 100 g of dry soil = 2*wsatiated_r  (Satiated water as measured on subareal soils is not wet enough for subaqueous soils, so a multiplier of 2 is employed)

The "b" variable depends on mineralogy and could be adjusted to reflect the component data.

Thus, for a layer:

n-value=(((2*wsatiated_r)-sandtotal_r)-(0.2*(silttotal_r+sandtotal_r)))/(claytotal_r+(3*om_r)  


Pons, L.J., and I.S. Zonneveld. 1965. Soil ripening and soil classification: Initial soil formation in alluvial deposits and a classification of the resulting soils. Publ. 13. Int. Inst. Land Reclamation and Improvement, Wageningen, The Netherlands.

Returns values for an rv: having a single value.

propname: Ksat entire profile travel time to 150 cm
description: Calculates the travel time in hours for water to move under saturated conditions thrugh the entire profile.  For each horizon, the horizon thickness in inches is divided by the RV Ksat (inches/hour).  These values are then summed to determine total  hours for water to move through the entire soil profile to a depth of 150 cm .  Organic duff horizons, bedrock, and cemented material are excluded from the travel time calculation.

Finds the of months for a component that do not have wet soil moisture status.


exec sql select comonth.month
from component, comonth
where join component to comonth
and not exists(select * from cosoilmoist where soimoiststat = "wet" and join cosoilmoist to comonth
and (taxtempcl in ("hypergelic", "pergelic", "subgelic") 
and comonth.month in ("jul", "aug"))

or (taxtempregime in ("thermic")
and comonth.month in ("feb", "mar", "apr", "may", "jun", "jul", "aug", "sep", "oct"))

or (taxtempregime in ("mesic")
and comonth.month in ("mar", "apr", "may", "jun", "jul", "aug", "sep", "oct"))

or (taxtempregime in ("cryic")
and comonth.month in ("jun", "jul", "aug"))

or (taxtempregime in ("frigid", "isofrigid") 
and comonth.month in ("may", "jun", "jul", "aug", "sep")) 

or (taxtempregime in ("hyperthermic") 
and comonth.month in ("feb", "mar", "apr", "may", "jun", "jul", "aug", "sep", "oct", "nov", "dec")) 

or (taxtempregime in ("isothermic", "isohyperthermic", "isomesic") 
and comonth.month in ("jan", "feb", "mar", "apr", "may", "jun", "jul", "aug", "sep", "oct", "nov", "dec")));
sort by comonth.month.

derive growth from rv using "NSSC Data":"GROWING SEASON NUMBER OF MONTHS".

# Label month code with month name.

define dry	ARRAYCOUNT(comonth.month).

define rv	dry/growth.

propname: DEPTH TO HIGH WATER TABLE APPARENT MINIMUM(EXP)
description:
Finds the top depth of a soil moisture layer of type "wet" or "saturation" that does have another layer below it of similar type.
 
Returns values of low, high, and rv for the depth to the top of the soil moisture: each can have multiple values, one for each month having an apparent water table.

Testing calculating a root sufficiency index.
Dan Childress  May 2009

Copied and modified somewhat from original.

Kiniry, L. N., C. L. Scrivner, M. E. Keener. 1983. A soil productivity index based upon predicted water depletion and root growth. Research Bulletin 1051. University of Missouri-Columbia. College of Agriculture. Agricultural Experiment Station.

Testing calculating a root sufficiency index.
Dan Childress  May 2009

Copied and modified somewhat form original.

# Determine the depth to the first restrictive layer 
DERIVE depth from rv using "NSSC Pangaea":"DEPTH TO FIRST RESTRICTION BELOW ORGANIC LAYER".
DERIVE o_thickness from rv using "NSSC Data":"SURFACE ORGANIC HORIZON THICKNESS, NOT HISTOSOL".

ASSIGN fragvol_r	REGROUP fragvol_r by hzname aggregate sum.
ASSIGN hzdept_r		REGROUP hzdept_r by hzname aggregate first.
ASSIGN hzdepb_r		REGROUP hzdepb_r by hzname aggregate first.
ASSIGN cec7_r		REGROUP cec7_r by hzname aggregate first.
ASSIGN ecec_r		REGROUP ecec_r by hzname aggregate first.
ASSIGN dbthirdbar_r	REGROUP dbthirdbar_r by hzname aggregate first.
ASSIGN hzname		REGROUP hzname by hzname aggregate first.


# Find minimum of restriction depth and 151cm.
DEFINE min_depth  depth < 151 and not isnull(depth) ? depth : 151.
 
# Find the thickness of each horizon between 0-151cm.
define top_in_range     hzdept_r > min_depth ? min_depth : hzdept_r - o_thickness.
define bottom_in_range  hzdepb_r > min_depth ? min_depth : hzdepb_r - o_thickness.
define layer_thickness  bottom_in_range - top_in_range.

taxonomic temperature regime	corresponding months
----------------------------	---------------------
cryic, isofrigid or pergelic	July and August

frigid or mesic			May, June, July, 
				August, and September

thermic 			March, April, May, 
			        June, July, August,
				September, and October
				
isothermic,			Jan., Feb., March, April,
isohyperthermic,		May, June, July, August,
                 		September, October, 
				November and December

isomesic, hyperthermic	        February, March, April,
		                May, June, July, August,
                		September, October, 
				November and December

Finds the maximum aluminum value for the component.
 
Returns max values for low,rv,high value.

Some agricultural crops suffer from aluminum toxicity when the Al saturation is only 10%. Aluminum interferes with the photosynthetic cycle by complexing with phosphate, so with high soluble aluminum the plant is starved for phosphate. Al-toxicity also stunts root growth thereby limiting the amount of soil the plant can exploit for nutrients. Stunted roots can also limit water uptake and can cause plants to wilt with only a few days without water. Some plants (e.g. cassava) have high tolerance to high levels of soluble aluminum. High soluble Al and acidity may adversely affect soil health by inhibiting beneficial organisms. When liming soils with high soluble aluminum the rule of thumb is to add 1.5 tons of CaCO3 per acre for every milliequivalents of soluble aluminum. The pH only needs to be raised to about 5.5 to eliminate the harmful effects of high soluble aluminum. (Source: Dr. Robert Gavenda, PhD; PowerPoint presentation on soil degradation)

About one-third of the tropics (1.5 billion hectares) has sufficiently strong soil acidity for soluble aluminum to be toxic to most crop species. This constraint is defined as having more than 60% Al saturation in some part of the top 50 cm of soil. A soil pH value of less than 5.5 usually indicates this problem (Evans and Kamprath, 1970). Aluminum toxicity is most prevalent in the humid tropics and acid savannas. This constraint is found mainly in soils classified as oxisols, ultisols and closely related inceptisols and is correlated with low nutrient capital reserves. Aluminum toxicity is usually the overwhelming constraint in these soils and must be tackled first, either by modern lime application practices, by using Al-tolerant plant species or by breeding for Al-tolerant varieties (Sanchez and Salinas, 1981). It is relevant to note that aluminum toxicity is rare in most smallholder farming areas of subhumid and semiarid Africa, except for parts of Rwanda, Burundi, Northern Zambia, Southern Congo, KwaZulu Natal Province in South Africa and in some sandy soils of Zimbabwe (Sanchez et al., 1997). Two-thirds of the tropics does not have enough aluminum saturation to worry about. Aluminum toxicity can become a positive soil quality attribute when using Al-tolerant plants in P-deficient soils. The low pH facilitates the dissolution of phosphate rocks, letting, in effect, the H+ ions in the soil do what a superphosphate factory doestreating rock phosphates with acids (Sanchez and Salinas, 1981). High aluminum saturation, as defined by this modifier, is also a positive attribute for rubber and tea production (Smith, 1989).  (Source: Fertility capability soil classification: a tool to help assess soil quality in the tropics by Pedro A. Sancheza,, Cheryl A. Palma, and Stanley W. Buol)

The citrate-bicarbonate-dithionite extractable iron content ("free iron oxides") of soil is significant in the chemistry and function of soil. propname: AVAILABLE WATER CAPACITY IN DEPTH 0-200cm - excludes duff
description:
Computes the total Available Water Capacity from the surface to 200 cm.  It excludes forest duff horizons with inlieu textures of "mpm","spm", "udom", "pdom", or "hpm". The total is computed by multiplying the horizon AWC by the horizon thickness for that portion of each horizon in the depth range, then summing across horizons.

Returns values for low, high, and rv: each has a single value.

propname: WATER TABLE INDEX DURING GROWING SEASON - NITRATE LEACHING
description:
Calculate a water table index based on wet soil moisture status during the months of April through October.  Only water table RV depths of 60 cm or less for components that are somewhat poorly, poorly, or very poorly drained are included in the calculation.

The formula is 200 - water table top depth RV for each month that a water table is present.  The value for each month is then summed to calculate the water table index.

Hydrologic group D, A/D, B/D, C/D - no adjustment

Data used:  hzdept_r, sieveno10_l, sieveno10_h, sieveno10_r, frag3to10_l, frag3to10_h, frag3to10_r, fraggt10_l, fraggt10_h and fraggt10_r from  the component, component horizon, and component restrictions tables.
	Considerations:
	1.  Depth to the top of the first restrictive layer;
	2.  Horizon depth;
	3.  Percent Passing the 10# sieve and
	4.  Percent coarse fragments > 3 inches.

Logic:  Finds the rv weighted average of rock fragments of size 2mm to <75mm  in all horizons above a  restrictive layer or within 150cm  of the surface.  Uses sieve and rock percents from the Horizon table.  Selects depth from horizons whose upper depth above a restrictive layer is within the 0 to 150 cm depth.  For horizons extending below 150 cm, the weighted average may be biased.

The 2mm to <75mm fragments are represented by the percent retained on the #10 sieve (100 - #10). This is adjusted for stones by multiplying it times the fraction less than 75mm (1 - (Rock 3-10 + Rock >10)/100).


Returns values for low, high, and rv: each has a single value.

Some agricultural crops suffer from aluminum toxicity when the Al saturation is only 10%. Aluminum interferes with the photosynthetic cycle by complexing with phosphate, so with high soluble aluminum the plant is starved for phosphate. Al-toxicity also stunts root growth thereby limiting the amount of soil the plant can exploit for nutrients. Stunted roots can also limit water uptake and can cause plants to wilt with only a few days without water. Some plants (e.g. cassava) have high tolerance to high levels of soluble aluminum. High soluble Al and acidity may adversely affect soil health by inhibiting beneficial organisms. When liming soils with high soluble aluminum the rule of thumb is to add 1.5 tons of CaCO3 per acre for every milliequivalents of soluble aluminum. The pH only needs to be raised to about 5.5 to eliminate the harmful effects of high soluble aluminum. (Source: Dr. Robert Gavenda, PhD; PowerPoint presentation on soil degradation)

About one-third of the tropics (1.5 billion hectares) has sufficiently strong soil acidity for soluble aluminum to be toxic to most crop species. This constraint is defined as having more than 60% Al saturation in some part of the top 50 cm of soil. A soil pH value of less than 5.5 usually indicates this problem (Evans and Kamprath, 1970). Aluminum toxicity is most prevalent in the humid tropics and acid savannas. This constraint is found mainly in soils classified as oxisols, ultisols and closely related inceptisols and is correlated with low nutrient capital reserves. Aluminum toxicity is usually the overwhelming constraint in these soils and must be tackled first, either by modern lime application practices, by using Al-tolerant plant species or by breeding for Al-tolerant varieties (Sanchez and Salinas, 1981). It is relevant to note that aluminum toxicity is rare in most smallholder farming areas of subhumid and semiarid Africa, except for parts of Rwanda, Burundi, Northern Zambia, Southern Congo, KwaZulu Natal Province in South Africa and in some sandy soils of Zimbabwe (Sanchez et al., 1997). Two-thirds of the tropics does not have enough aluminum saturation to worry about. Aluminum toxicity can become a positive soil quality attribute when using Al-tolerant plants in P-deficient soils. The low pH facilitates the dissolution of phosphate rocks, letting, in effect, the H+ ions in the soil do what a superphosphate factory doestreating rock phosphates with acids (Sanchez and Salinas, 1981). High aluminum saturation, as defined by this modifier, is also a positive attribute for rubber and tea production (Smith, 1989).  (Source: Fertility capability soil classification: a tool to help assess soil quality in the tropics by Pedro A. Sancheza,, Cheryl A. Palma, and Stanley W. Buol)

Finds the maximum aluminum value for the component.
 
Returns max values for low,rv,high value.

Some agricultural crops suffer from aluminum toxicity when the Al saturation is only 10%. Aluminum interferes with the photosynthetic cycle by complexing with phosphate, so with high soluble aluminum the plant is starved for phosphate. Al-toxicity also stunts root growth thereby limiting the amount of soil the plant can exploit for nutrients. Stunted roots can also limit water uptake and can cause plants to wilt with only a few days without water. Some plants (e.g. cassava) have high tolerance to high levels of soluble aluminum. High soluble Al and acidity may adversely affect soil health by inhibiting beneficial organisms. When liming soils with high soluble aluminum the rule of thumb is to add 1.5 tons of CaCO3 per acre for every milliequivalents of soluble aluminum. The pH only needs to be raised to about 5.5 to eliminate the harmful effects of high soluble aluminum. (Source: Dr. Robert Gavenda, PhD; PowerPoint presentation on soil degradation)

About one-third of the tropics (1.5 billion hectares) has sufficiently strong soil acidity for soluble aluminum to be toxic to most crop species. This constraint is defined as having more than 60% Al saturation in some part of the top 50 cm of soil. A soil pH value of less than 5.5 usually indicates this problem (Evans and Kamprath, 1970). Aluminum toxicity is most prevalent in the humid tropics and acid savannas. This constraint is found mainly in soils classified as oxisols, ultisols and closely related inceptisols and is correlated with low nutrient capital reserves. Aluminum toxicity is usually the overwhelming constraint in these soils and must be tackled first, either by modern lime application practices, by using Al-tolerant plant species or by breeding for Al-tolerant varieties (Sanchez and Salinas, 1981). It is relevant to note that aluminum toxicity is rare in most smallholder farming areas of subhumid and semiarid Africa, except for parts of Rwanda, Burundi, Northern Zambia, Southern Congo, KwaZulu Natal Province in South Africa and in some sandy soils of Zimbabwe (Sanchez et al., 1997). Two-thirds of the tropics does not have enough aluminum saturation to worry about. Aluminum toxicity can become a positive soil quality attribute when using Al-tolerant plants in P-deficient soils. The low pH facilitates the dissolution of phosphate rocks, letting, in effect, the H+ ions in the soil do what a superphosphate factory doestreating rock phosphates with acids (Sanchez and Salinas, 1981). High aluminum saturation, as defined by this modifier, is also a positive attribute for rubber and tea production (Smith, 1989).  (Source: Fertility capability soil classification: a tool to help assess soil quality in the tropics by Pedro A. Sancheza,, Cheryl A. Palma, and Stanley W. Buol)
