Criteria used in the estimate is from NSSH 618.49(c).

Data elements used include slope RV, Ksat RV, and soil moisture depth low, rv, and high.  To attempt to determine "concave" settings, slope shape across and down are looked at as is ponding frequency.

Known limitations:  Not all soils in concave settings will be found.  Therefore their rating may be in error.

Liquefaction susceptibility depends on having saturated unconsolidated sediments on a nearly level surface when the ground shakes. 

Younger deposits are more susceptible than older deposits.  Soil order is used as a proxy for age.  This scale, as are the others, is debatable. 

The materials must be saturated.  The presence of an apparent water table is used as an indicator of saturation.  It is entirely possible the saturation can exist below the soil survey frame of reference and thus be undetected.  

The materials must be unconsolidated.  Some materials are more unconsolidated than others, due to their environment and mode of deposition.

Generally, surfaces that liquify are flat, so slope is a factor.

Finds the maximum aluminum value for the component.
 
Returns max values for low,rv,high value.

Some agricultural crops suffer from aluminum toxicity when the Al saturation is only 10%. Aluminum interferes with the photosynthetic cycle by complexing with phosphate, so with high soluble aluminum the plant is starved for phosphate. Al-toxicity also stunts root growth thereby limiting the amount of soil the plant can exploit for nutrients. Stunted roots can also limit water uptake and can cause plants to wilt with only a few days without water. Some plants (e.g. cassava) have high tolerance to high levels of soluble aluminum. High soluble Al and acidity may adversely affect soil health by inhibiting beneficial organisms. When liming soils with high soluble aluminum the rule of thumb is to add 1.5 tons of CaCO3 per acre for every milliequivalents of soluble aluminum. The pH only needs to be raised to about 5.5 to eliminate the harmful effects of high soluble aluminum. (Source: Dr. Robert Gavenda, PhD; PowerPoint presentation on soil degradation)

About one-third of the tropics (1.5 billion hectares) has sufficiently strong soil acidity for soluble aluminum to be toxic to most crop species. This constraint is defined as having more than 60% Al saturation in some part of the top 50 cm of soil. A soil pH value of less than 5.5 usually indicates this problem (Evans and Kamprath, 1970). Aluminum toxicity is most prevalent in the humid tropics and acid savannas. This constraint is found mainly in soils classified as oxisols, ultisols and closely related inceptisols and is correlated with low nutrient capital reserves. Aluminum toxicity is usually the overwhelming constraint in these soils and must be tackled first, either by modern lime application practices, by using Al-tolerant plant species or by breeding for Al-tolerant varieties (Sanchez and Salinas, 1981). It is relevant to note that aluminum toxicity is rare in most smallholder farming areas of subhumid and semiarid Africa, except for parts of Rwanda, Burundi, Northern Zambia, Southern Congo, KwaZulu Natal Province in South Africa and in some sandy soils of Zimbabwe (Sanchez et al., 1997). Two-thirds of the tropics do not have enough aluminum saturation to worry about. Aluminum toxicity can become a positive soil quality attribute when using Al-tolerant plants in P-deficient soils. The low pH facilitates the dissolution of phosphate rocks, letting, in effect, the H+ ions in the soil do what a superphosphate factory doestreating rock phosphates with acids (Sanchez and Salinas, 1981). High aluminum saturation, as defined by this modifier, is also a positive attribute for rubber and tea production (Smith, 1989).  (Source: Fertility capability soil classification: a tool to help assess soil quality in the tropics by Pedro A. Sancheza,, Cheryl A. Palma, and Stanley W. Buol)

This script looks for the phrase *limeston*residuum* to return any soil that may be residual over limestone.  Also, the taxonomic great group is examined for the "Pale" feature.  The map unit name and local phase are examined for "karst".  A numeric rating is returned for various combinations of these, as shown below:


If the parent material is limestone residuum and the soil is in a "Pale" great group, then the rating is .1.

If the parent material is limestone residuum and the soil is in a "Pale" great group and either the map unit name or the local phase indicates "karst", then the rating is .4.

If the parent material is limestone residuum then the rating is .5.

If the parent material is limestone residuum and  either the map unit name or the local phase indicates "karst", then the rating is .8.

Finds the sum of the estimated reserve acidity for oxidized soil for horizons that have a top depth <=200cm.

The oxidized pH is an estimator of the proportion af acidic ions (Al, H) in a layer.   The CEC_7 is an estimator of the reserve acidity.  There is no measure of the non-exchangeable (mineral) acidity.  It is assumed all the sulfidic material oxidizes during the incubation.  The n-value is used as an estimator of the amount of soil present, since much of the volume of a subaqueous soil is water.  Higher n-value is more fluidic, meaning more water in the soil.

The units on the derived number are muddled at best; thus, the result is best thought of as an index of potential acidity.

Returns a value for the rv.

Testing calculating a root sufficiency index.
Dan Childress  May 2009

Hydric Soil Categories

This Hydric Soil Category rating indicates the components of map units that meet the criteria for hydric soils. Map units are composed of one or more major soil components or soil types that generally make up 20 percent or more of the map unit and are listed in the map unit name, and they may also have one or more minor contrasting soil components that generally make up less than 20 percent of the map unit. Each major and minor map unit component that meets the hydric criteria is rated hydric. The map unit class ratings based on the hydric components present are: TN Hydric, TN Predominantly Hydric, TN Partially Hydric, TN Predominantly Nonhydric, and TN Nonhydric. The report also shows the total representative percentage of each map unit that the hydric components comprise.

"TN Hydric" means that all major and minor components listed for a given map unit are rated as being hydric. "TN Predominantly Hydric" means that all major components listed for a given map unit are rated as hydric, and at least one contrasting minor component is not rated hydric."TN Partially Hydric" means that at least one major component listed for a given map unit is rated as hydric, and at least one other major component is not rated hydric. "TN Predominantly Nonhydric" means that no major component listed for a given map unit is rated as hydric, and at least one contrasting minor component is rated hydric. "TN Nonhydric" means no major or minor components for the map unit are rated hydric. The assumption is that the map unit is nonhydric even if none of the components within the map unit have been rated.

Hydric soils are defined by the National Technical Committee for Hydric Soils (NTCHS) as soils that formed under conditions of saturation, flooding, or ponding long enough during the growing season to develop anaerobic conditions in the upper part (Federal Register, 1994). Under natural conditions, these soils are either saturated or inundated long enough during the growing season to support the growth and reproduction of hydrophytic vegetation.

If soils are wet enough for a long enough period of time to be considered hydric, they typically exhibit certain properties that can be easily observed in the field. These visible properties are indicators of hydric soils. The indicators used to make onsite determinations of hydric soils are specified in "Field Indicators of Hydric Soils in the United States" (Vasilas, Hurt, and Noble, 2010).

The NTCHS has developed criteria to identify those soil properties unique to hydric soils (Federal Register, 2012). These criteria are used to identify map unit components that normally are associated with wetlands. The criteria use selected soil properties that are described in Field Indicators of Hydric Soils in the United States (Vasilas, Hurt, and Noble, 2010), "Soil Taxonomy" (Soil Survey Staff, 1999), "Keys to Soil Taxonomy" (Soil Survey Staff, 2010), and the "Soil Survey Manual" (Soil Survey Division Staff, 1993).

The criteria for hydric soils are represented by codes, for example, 2 or 3. Definitions for the codes are as follows:

All Histels except for Folistels, and Histosols except for Folists.

Soils in Aquic suborders, great groups, or subgroups, Albolls suborder, Historthels great group, Histoturbels great group, Pachic subgroups, or Cumulic subgroups that:

Based on the range of characteristics for the soil series, will at least in part meet one or more Field Indicators of Hydric Soils in the United States, or

Show evidence that the soil meets the definition of a hydric soil;

Soils that are frequently ponded for long or very long duration during the growing season.

Based on the range of characteristics for the soil series, will at least in part meet one or more Field Indicators of Hydric Soils in the United States, or

Show evidence that the soil meets the definition of a hydric soil;

Map unit components that are frequently flooded for long duration or very long duration during the growing season that:

Based on the range of characteristics for the soil series, will at least in part meet one or more Field Indicators of Hydric Soils in the United States, or

Show evidence that the soil meets the definition of a hydric soil;

Hydric Condition: Food Security Act information regarding the ability to grow a commodity crop without removing woody vegetation or manipulating hydrology.

References:

Federal Register. July 13, 1994. Changes in hydric soils of the United States.
Federal Register. February, 28, 2012. Hydric soils of the United States.
Soil Survey Division Staff. 1993. Soil survey manual. Soil Conservation Service. U.S. Department of Agriculture Handbook 18.
Soil Survey Staff. 1999. Soil taxonomy: A basic system of soil classification for making and interpreting soil surveys. 2nd edition. Natural Resources Conservation Service. U.S. Department of Agriculture Handbook 436.
Soil Survey Staff. 2010. Keys to soil taxonomy. 11th edition. U.S. Department of Agriculture, Natural Resources Conservation Service.
Vasilas, L.M., G.W. Hurt, and C.V. Noble, editors. Version 7.0, 2010. Field indicators of hydric soils in the United States.

propname: GENERAL INDICATOR MLRA DURING < 135 FFD (2 C WARMING)
description:
Finds the of months for a component that do not have wet soil moisture status.


exec sql select comonth.month
from component, comonth
where join component to comonth
and not exists(select * from cosoilmoist where soimoiststat = "wet" and join cosoilmoist to comonth
and (taxtempcl in ("hypergelic", "pergelic", "subgelic") 
and comonth.month in ("jul", "aug"))

or (taxtempregime in ("thermic")
and comonth.month in ("feb", "mar", "apr", "may", "jun", "jul", "aug", "sep", "oct"))

or (taxtempregime in ("mesic")
and comonth.month in ("mar", "apr", "may", "jun", "jul", "aug", "sep", "oct"))

or (taxtempregime in ("cryic")
and comonth.month in ("jun", "jul", "aug"))

or (taxtempregime in ("frigid", "isofrigid") 
and comonth.month in ("may", "jun", "jul", "aug", "sep")) 

or (taxtempregime in ("hyperthermic") 
and comonth.month in ("feb", "mar", "apr", "may", "jun", "jul", "aug", "sep", "oct", "nov", "dec")) 

or (taxtempregime in ("isothermic", "isohyperthermic", "isomesic") 
and comonth.month in ("jan", "feb", "mar", "apr", "may", "jun", "jul", "aug", "sep", "oct", "nov", "dec")));
sort by comonth.month.

derive growth from rv using "NSSC Data":"GROWING SEASON NUMBER OF MONTHS".

propname: SVI - Leaching Risk with RF modification
description:
Resource Assessment Divisions's  (RAD) Soil Vulnerability Index factor for Leaching Risk criteria as provided to interpretations staff May 2014. To be used to test data in NASIS.

SVI leaching uses the following soil attributes:
1.	Hydrologic Group (hydgrp)
2.	Slope (slope_r)
3.	Erodibility Factor  fragment free (kffact)
4.	Surface Rock Fragment content (100  sieve10_r)
Soil Vulnerability for Leaching Risk and Runoff Risk by Soil Mapping Units	
	
Leaching Risk:	
("hydgrp" LIKE 'A%' AND "slope_r" <= 12) OR ("hydgrp" LIKE 'B%' AND "slope_r" < 3 AND "kffactfrev" < 0.24)                                                                                            leach = 4  (High)
("hydgrp" LIKE 'A%' AND "slope_r" > 12) OR ("hydgrp" LIKE 'B%' AND "slope_r" >= 3 AND "slope_r" <= 12 AND "kffactfrev" < 0.24)                                                         leach = 3  (Moderately high)
("hydgrp" LIKE 'B%' AND "slope_r" <= 12 AND "kffactfrev" >= 0.24) OR ("hydgrp" LIKE 'B%' AND "slope_r" > 12) OR ("hydgrp" LIKE 'C%')                                               leach = 2  (Moderate)
"hydgrp" LIKE 'D%'                                                                                                               	                                                                                                                            leach = 1  (Low)
	
Leaching modification for coarse fragment content of top layer:
	
"leach" = 1  AND "sievno10rf" >= 30	leachrev = 3 (Raised by two)
"leach" = 2  AND "sievno10rf" >= 30	leachrev = 4 (Raised by two)
"leach" = 3  AND "sievno10rf" >= 30	leachrev = 4 (Raised by one)
"leach" = 1  AND "sievno10rf" >= 10 AND "sievno10rf" < 30	leachrev = 2 (Raised by one)
"leach" = 2  AND "sievno10rf" >= 10 AND "sievno10rf" < 30	leachrev = 3 (Raised by one)
"leach" = 3  AND "sievno10rf" >= 10 AND "sievno10rf" < 30	leachrev = 4 (Raised by one)

Soil Vulnerability Indices (SVI) were first developed by the NRCS Resource Assessment Division (RAD) staff to help organize a national collection of soil attributes for the CEAP project in 2009.  CEAP modeling involves farmer survey data, along with soils information at each sample point as input into the Agricultural Policy / Environmental Extender or APEX model.   Farmers report on a range of farming and conservation practices (such as chemical use, tillage methods, application timing, rotations, use of buffer strips, conservation tillage, cover crops, etc.), and weather data for the previous three years in each field where NRI-CEAP sample data points are located.  This allows the CEAP team to make estimates of potential excess nutrients and sediments delivered into the environment, given a particular growing system, region and soil type.
 
 For each CEAP point, the APEX model produces a continuous rating of vulnerability from high to low risk for excess nutrient or sediment delivery, absent effective conservation under typical growing conditions.  The SVI for leaching (SVIleaching) can be used to group the CEAP nutrient loss risk results and the SVI for runoff (SVIrunoff) to group both the CEAP sediment and nutrient loss risk results.In addition to the CEAP application, the SVI is becoming a popular way to understand inherent soil vulnerability by many different initiatives and programs including those with many Federal, State, Local, Private, and Research stakeholders.

Resource Assessment Divisions's  (RAD) Soil Vulnerability Index factor criteria for Runoff Risk as provided to interpretations staff May 2014. To be used to test data in NASIS. No class limit documentation was provided at that time.

SVI leaching uses the following soil attributes:
1.	Hydrologic Group (hydgrp)
2.	Slope (slope_r)
3.	Erodibility Factor-fragment free (kffact)

Runoff Risk (As provided by RAD):  
	
("hydgrp" LIKE 'B%' AND "slope_r" > 6) OR ("hydgrp" LIKE 'C%' AND  "slope_r" > 6) OR ("hydgrp" LIKE 'D%' AND "slope_r" > 4)	runof = 4 (High)
("hydgrp" LIKE 'B%' AND "slope_r" >= 4 AND "slope_r" <= 6 AND "kffactfrev" >= 0.32 ) OR ("hydgrp" LIKE 'C%' AND "slope_r" >= 2 AND "slope_r" <= 6 AND "kffactfrev" >= 0.28) OR ("hydgrp" LIKE 'D%' AND "slope_r" >= 2 AND "slope_r" <= 4)  	runof = 3 (Moderately High)
("hydgrp" LIKE 'B%' AND "slope_r" >= 4 AND "slope_r" <= 6 AND "kffactfrev" < 0.32) OR  ("hydgrp" LIKE 'C%' AND "slope_r" >= 2 AND "slope_r" <= 6 AND "kffactfrev" < 0.28) OR ("hydgrp" LIKE 'D%' AND "slope_r" < 2 AND "kffactfrev" >= 0.28)         	runof = 2 (Moderate)
("hydgrp" LIKE 'A%') OR ("hydgrp" LIKE 'B%' AND "slope_r"  < 4) OR ("hydgrp" LIKE 'C%' AND "slope_r" < 2 ) OR ("hydgrp" LIKE 'D%' AND "slope_r" < 2 AND "kffactfrev" < 0.28)	runof = 1 (Low)

			(CODENAME(shapeacross) matches "concave" AND

			(CODENAME(shapeacross) matches "concave" AND

			CODENAME(shapedown) matches "concave") THEN 4.0

			(CODENAME(shapeacross) matches "linear" AND
			CODENAME(shapedown) matches "linear") THEN 5.0

			CODENAME(shapedown) matches "convex") THEN 6.0

			(CODENAME(shapeacross) matches "convex" AND
			CODENAME(shapedown) matches "convex") THEN 7.0

			(CODENAME(shapeacross) matches "convex" AND
			CODENAME(shapedown) matches "linear") THEN 8.0

			(CODENAME(shapeacross) matches "convex" AND
			CODENAME(shapedown) matches "concave") THEN 9.0

propname: xpete SOC (kg/m2) to 2 m bedrock/duripan or petro* (NPS)
description:
Evaluates soil organic carbon (SOC) to a depth of two meters or to the occurrence of any type of bedrock or other certain types of restrictive layers. 


rev. SBSouthard 10/09
SBSouthard 3/2009

1. Soil organic carbon result is in kg/m2 to the depth of the soil.  Conversion to pounds/acre: (kg/m) X (2.2 lbs/kg) X (4047 m2/acre); so, kg/m X 8903 = pounds SOC/acre. Likewise, kg/m2 * 4.4515 = tons/acre.

2. This rule evaluates to 2 meter depth or to representative top depth of any bedrock kind, any petro horizon and any duripan. Other types of restrictions were not coded into the depth to restriction subproperty used in the main interpretation property script because the concern is not rooting depth restrictions but total amount of SOC stabilized in soils on a volumetric basis. It was decided to include stabilized soil organic carbon that may exist below a strongly contrasted particle size. In a Fluvent, for example, or buried old surfaces below tephra deposits there may be large stores of carbon that lie below other kinds of restrictive layers.

3. The calculation reports on a volumetric whole soil basis, corrected for representative rock fragments in database. The representative amount of soil passing the #10 sieve, rock fragment particle density, and the representative 1/3 bar density of the soil is given priority. If sieves and RF weights are NULL the rock fragment volume table is used instead. The soil organic carbon is converted from horizon soil organic matter content stored as a weight percent of the < 2mm fraction of the soil and recalculated on a whole soil basis. If soil organic matter in the database is NULL, SOC is assumed to be zero.

4. The NPS SOC class rule attached to this property was designed using an arbitrary linear curve in the associated evaluation. The curve was designed so that the "fuzzy value" multiplied by 1000 gives you that actual amount SOC calculated for the component in the NASIS data. Units are kg/meter2 to some depth when multiplied by 1000 for the rule.

Data issues:

1. NULL 1/3 bulk density may exist for mineral horizons and this calculation will assign a bulk density value of 0.2 because in most cases NULL 1/3 bulk density in the data occurs with O horizons. Using this assumption, in some cases the amount of SOC will be underestimated for non-organic horizons with no bulk density populated.

2. Particle densities vary over the country but 2.65 was used universally. More complex default queries could be written using parent material. It is not apparent if map results with broad SOC classes would reflect the extra effort to refine particle densities. This will result in either overestimation or underestimation of SOC depending on rock type. The property script can be copied and edited for particle densities for individual areas.

3. An alternative subproperty script was added in October 2009 to use the horizon rock fragment volume table instead of sieves if sieves, RF 3-10" and >10" data columns are NULL.

Uses the structure class placement in Table 3 of the soil quality morphology index (Seybold et al., 2004). 

Table 3 places structure into 5 classes (1 - 5) with 5 having the best structure class for transmitting air and water, and root growth. In other words, the best soil quality (theoretically). 

Structure                          Criteria
  Class	
    5          Strong granular, strong very fine through medium blocky and very fine prismatic; 
                surface "O" horizons (structure is not applicable to organic layers); if soil structure is
                null and OM > 10%
    4          Moderate granular, moderate very fine and fine blocky; strong fine.
    3          Moderate medium blocky; very fine, fine and medium prismatic; strong very coarse
                and coarse blocky.
    2          Weak granular; moderate very coarse and coarse blocky; coarse and medium prismatic; 
                strong very coarse and coarse prismatic; weak platy; weak lenticular.
    1          All other soil structures (includes columnar, wedge, cloddy, massive, and single grain).

Seybold, C.A., R.B. Grossman, H. Hoper, G. Muckel, and D.L. Karlen. 2004. Soil quality morphological index measured in the 1996 NRI pilot study. Soil Survey Horizons 45(3):86-95.

propname: SOC (kg/m2) to 2 m bedrock/duripan or petro* (0 to 30)
description:
Evaluates soil organic carbon (SOC) to a depth of two meters or to the occurrence of any type of bedrock or other certain types of restrictive layers. 


rev. SBSouthard 10/09
SBSouthard 3/2009

1. Soil organic carbon result is in kg/m2 to the depth of the soil.  Conversion to pounds/acre: (kg/m) X (2.2 lbs/kg) X (4047 m2/acre); so, kg/m X 8903 = pounds SOC/acre. Likewise, kg/m2 * 4.4515 = tons/acre.

2. This rule evaluates to 2 meter depth or to representative top depth of any bedrock kind, any petro horizon and any duripan. Other types of restrictions were not coded into the depth to restriction subproperty used in the main interpretation property script because the concern is not rooting depth restrictions but total amount of SOC stabilized in soils on a volumetric basis. It was decided to include stabilized soil organic carbon that may exist below a strongly contrasted particle size. In a Fluvent, for example, or buried old surfaces below tephra deposits there may be large stores of carbon that lie below other kinds of restrictive layers.

3. The calculation reports on a volumetric whole soil basis, corrected for representative rock fragments in database. The representative amount of soil passing the #10 sieve, rock fragment particle density, and the representative 1/3 bar density of the soil is given priority. If sieves and RF weights are NULL the rock fragment volume table is used instead. The soil organic carbon is converted from horizon soil organic matter content stored as a weight percent of the < 2mm fraction of the soil and recalculated on a whole soil basis. If soil organic matter in the database is NULL, SOC is assumed to be zero.

4. The NPS SOC class rule attached to this property was designed using an arbitrary linear curve in the associated evaluation. The curve was designed so that the "fuzzy value" multiplied by 1000 gives you that actual amount SOC calculated for the component in the NASIS data. Units are kg/meter2 to some depth when multiplied by 1000 for the rule.

Data issues:

1. NULL 1/3 bulk density may exist for mineral horizons and this calculation will assign a bulk density value of 0.2 because in most cases NULL 1/3 bulk density in the data occurs with O horizons. Using this assumption, in some cases the amount of SOC will be underestimated for non-organic horizons with no bulk density populated.

2. Particle densities vary over the country but 2.65 was used universally. More complex default queries could be written using parent material. It is not apparent if map results with broad SOC classes would reflect the extra effort to refine particle densities. This will result in either overestimation or underestimation of SOC depending on rock type. The property script can be copied and edited for particle densities for individual areas.

3. An alternative subproperty script was added in October 2009 to use the horizon rock fragment volume table instead of sieves if sieves, RF 3-10" and >10" data columns are NULL.

propname: SQL-SOC (kg/m2) to 2 m bedrock/duripan or petro
description:
Evaluates soil organic carbon (SOC) to a depth of two meters or to the occurrence of any type of bedrock or other certain types of restrictive layers. 


rev. SBSouthard 10/09
SBSouthard 3/2009

1. Soil organic carbon result is in kg/m2 to the depth of the soil.  Conversion to pounds/acre: (kg/m) X (2.2 lbs/kg) X (4047 m2/acre); so, kg/m X 8903 = pounds SOC/acre. Likewise, kg/m2 * 4.4515 = tons/acre.

2. This rule evaluates to 2 meter depth or to representative top depth of any bedrock kind, any petro horizon and any duripan. Other types of restrictions were not coded into the depth to restriction subproperty used in the main interpretation property script because the concern is not rooting depth restrictions but total amount of SOC stabilized in soils on a volumetric basis. It was decided to include stabilized soil organic carbon that may exist below a strongly contrasted particle size. In a Fluvent, for example, or buried old surfaces below tephra deposits there may be large stores of carbon that lie below other kinds of restrictive layers.

3. The calculation reports on a volumetric whole soil basis, corrected for representative rock fragments in database. The representative amount of soil passing the #10 sieve, rock fragment particle density, and the representative 1/3 bar density of the soil is given priority. If sieves and RF weights are NULL the rock fragment volume table is used instead. The soil organic carbon is converted from horizon soil organic matter content stored as a weight percent of the < 2mm fraction of the soil and recalculated on a whole soil basis. If soil organic matter in the database is NULL, SOC is assumed to be zero.

4. The NPS SOC class rule attached to this property was designed using an arbitrary linear curve in the associated evaluation. The curve was designed so that the "fuzzy value" multiplied by 1000 gives you that actual amount SOC calculated for the component in the NASIS data. Units are kg/meter2 to some depth when multiplied by 1000 for the rule.

Data issues:

1. NULL 1/3 bulk density may exist for mineral horizons and this calculation will assign a bulk density value of 0.2 because in most cases NULL 1/3 bulk density in the data occurs with O horizons. Using this assumption, in some cases the amount of SOC will be underestimated for non-organic horizons with no bulk density populated.

2. Particle densities vary over the country but 2.65 was used universally. More complex default queries could be written using parent material. It is not apparent if map results with broad SOC classes would reflect the extra effort to refine particle densities. This will result in either overestimation or underestimation of SOC depending on rock type. The property script can be copied and edited for particle densities for individual areas.

3. An alternative subproperty script was added in October 2009 to use the horizon rock fragment volume table instead of sieves if sieves, RF 3-10" and >10" data columns are NULL.

This property uses Hamon 1963 to find potential evapotranspiration.  It uses the Latitude Estimator to find the declination.  Mean annual air temperature is used in calculating the vapor pressure.  The monthly mean temperature  is estimated using the Latitude Estimator and Continentality.

Calculates an approximation of PET using Hamon (1963).

 PET= k*0.165*217.7*N*(es/(T+273.3))

WHERE,
 PET = potential evapotranspiration [mm day-1]
 k = proportionality coefficient = 11 [unitless]
 N = daytime length [x/12 hours]
 N = (24/pi)*w
 es = saturation vapor pressure [mb]
 T = average monthly temperature [C]
 es = saturation vapor pressure
 es = 6.108e(17.27T/(T+273.3))
 w = invcos(-tan(d)tan(phi))
 phi = latitude in radians
 d = declination in radians
 d = 1 + 0.033cos(2*pi*j/365)
  j = julian day of the year

Reference: Hamon, W. R., 1963. Computation of direct runoff amounts from storm rainfall.  Int Assoc. Sci. Hydrol. Pub 63:52-62.

Calculates the Mean Annual Precipitation minus the potential evapotranspiration using an equation as close to Hamon (1963) as was possible.  Result is mm per FFD.  Can be negative in dry climates.  A single value for the rv is returned.

This property uses Hamon 1963 to find potential evapotranspiration.  It uses the Latitude Estimator to find the declination.  Mean annual air temperature is used in calculating the vapor pressure.  The monthly mean temperature  is estimated using the Latitude Estimator and Continentality.

Calculates an approximation of PET using Hamon (1963).

 PET= k*0.165*217.7*N*(es/(T+273.3))
where,
 PET= potential evapotranspiration [mm day-1]
 k= proportionality coefficient = 11 [unitless]
 N= daytime length [x/12 hours]
N = (24/pi)*w
es= saturation vapor pressure [mb]
T= average monthly temperature [C]
es = saturation vapor pressure
 es=6.108e(17.27T/(T+273.3))
 w = invcos(-tan(d)tan(phi))
 phi = latitude in radians
 d = declination in radians
 d= 1 + 0.033cos(2*pi*j/365)
 j is julian day of the year

propname: DEPTH TO WATER TABLE IN GROWING SEASON INDEX
description:
Gets the average water table depth (where soil moisture is "wet") within the growing season scaled from 0.5 to 1.5 (> 1.52cm depth = 0.5)

Growing season months are derived from the temperature regime of the soil component as follows:

Temperature Regime	               Growing Season Months
------------------	                               ---------------------
cryic, pergelic, isofrigid	                July and August
frigid, mesic		                May, June, July, August, and September
thermic, hyperthermic	                April, May, June, Ju ly, August, September, and October
isothermic, sohyperthermic, isomesic	February, March, April, May, June, July, August, September, October, and November

The De Martonne (1926) aridity index (AI) uses temperature as a proxy for evapotransporation as follows: AI = P / (T + 10)
Where P (mm) is the annual precip and T (Celcius) the mean annual air temperature.
The equation is appropriate for temperatures > -9.9 C.
The AI decreases (approaches zero) with increasing aridity.

Finds the component Mean Annual Percipitation(MAP) converted from mm to cm.

Returns values for low, high and rv: each set to same as rv value.

Logic:  Finds the weighted average percentage of rock fragments of size greater than 75mm in the horizons above a restrictive feature or from 0 to 180 cm deep.  Uses the rock percents from the Horizon table.

To compute a weighted average, the sum of rock  > 75mm for each horizon is multiplied by the horizon thickness, then averaged over all horizons above a restrictive feature or to 91 cm.

Computes the weighted average of the ratio CEC / Clay %.  Computed by multiplying the CEC / Clay ratio for each horizon by the ratio of the horizon thickness in the depth range 61 to 91 cm.
 
Returns a single value for the rv only:  The high and low values that result from this calculation are meaningless because these calculations result in numbers that are not monotonic in nature.  In some cases the low is greater than either the high or the rv.  In others the rv is greater than the low and high calculation and in other cases the high is greater than the low but less than the rv.  Upon analysis of the intent and purpose of this property in relation to the interpretive evaluation and rule the decision was made to use the rv only.  Bob Nielsen 7/98.

Use this calculation to estimate Runoff class in the Component table.  

Criteria used in the estimate is from NSSH 618.49(c).

Data elements used include slope RV, Ksat RV, and soil moisture depth low, rv, and high.  To attempt to determine "concave" settings, slope shape across and down are looked at as is ponding frequency.

Note: We did not include any adjustment to the table in NSSH based on depth to minimum Ksat as suggested by NSSH narrative as this produced unreasonable results.  NSSH will be updated accordingly.

Known limitations:  Not all soils in concave settings will be found.  Therefore their rating may be in error.

A single value is returned for the runoff class.

This is Paul Finnell's calculation modified into a property script.

Calculates the USLE erosion index of rkls/t.


DEFINE slopelen		IF slope_r >= 0 and slope_r < 0.75 THEN 100
                    ELSE IF slope_r >= 0.75 and slope_r < 1.5 THEN 200
                    ELSE IF slope_r >= 1.5 and slope_r < 2.5 THEN 300
                    ELSE IF slope_r >= 2.5 and slope_r < 3.5 THEN 200
                    ELSE IF slope_r >= 3.5 and slope_r < 4.5 THEN 180
                    ELSE IF slope_r >= 4.5 and slope_r < 5.5 THEN 160
                    ELSE IF slope_r >= 5.5 and slope_r < 6.5 THEN 150
                    ELSE IF slope_r >= 6.5 and slope_r < 7.5 THEN 140
                    ELSE IF slope_r >= 7.5 and slope_r < 8.5 THEN 130
                    ELSE IF slope_r >= 8.5 and slope_r < 9.5 THEN 125
                    ELSE IF slope_r >= 9.5 and slope_r < 10.5 THEN 120
                    ELSE IF slope_r >= 10.5 and slope_r < 11.5 THEN 110
                    ELSE IF slope_r >= 11.5 and slope_r < 12.5 THEN 100
                    ELSE IF slope_r >= 12.5 and slope_r < 13.5 THEN 90
                    ELSE IF slope_r >= 13.5 and slope_r < 14.5 THEN 80
                    ELSE IF slope_r >= 14.5 and slope_r < 15.5 THEN 70
                    ELSE IF slope_r >= 15.5 and slope_r < 17.5 THEN 60
                    ELSE IF slope_r >= 17.5 THEN 50
					ELSE null.

# Uses Palouse region slope length lookup table (feet).
DEFINE slopelen_palouse		IF slope_r >= 0 and slope_r < 5.5 THEN 350
                    		ELSE IF slope_r >= 5.5 and slope_r < 10.5 THEN 275
                    		ELSE IF slope_r >= 10.5 and slope_r < 15.5 THEN 225
                    		ELSE IF slope_r >= 15.5 and slope_r < 20.5 THEN 175
                    		ELSE IF slope_r >= 20.5 and slope_r < 25.5 THEN 150
                    		ELSE IF slope_r >= 25.5 and slope_r < 35.5 THEN 125
                    		ELSE IF slope_r >= 35.5 THEN 100
							ELSE null.

define palouse		if areasymbol imatches 'ID620' then 1 else if
					areasymbol imatches 'ID057' then 1 else if
					areasymbol imatches 'OR021' then 1 else if
					areasymbol imatches 'OR049' then 1 else if
					areasymbol imatches 'OR055' then 1 else if
					areasymbol imatches 'OR625' then 1 else if
					areasymbol imatches 'OR667' then 1 else if
					areasymbol imatches 'OR670' then 1 else if
					areasymbol imatches 'OR673' then 1 else if
					areasymbol imatches 'WA001' then 1 else if
 					areasymbol imatches 'WA021' then 1 else if
					areasymbol imatches 'WA025' then 1 else if
					areasymbol imatches 'WA043' then 1 else if
					areasymbol imatches 'WA063' then 1 else if
					areasymbol imatches 'WA071' then 1 else if
					areasymbol imatches 'WA075' then 1 else if
					areasymbol imatches 'WA603' then 1 else if
					areasymbol imatches 'WA605' then 1 else if
					areasymbol imatches 'WA613' then 1 else if
					areasymbol imatches 'WA617' then 1 else if
					areasymbol imatches 'WA623' then 1 else if
					areasymbol imatches 'WA639' then 1 else if
					areasymbol imatches 'WA676' then 1 else if
					areasymbol imatches 'WA677' then 1 else 0.
define explanation	"Slope length units are feet.".
define slope_length			if palouse == 0 then slopelen else if
					palouse == 1 then slopelen_palouse else slopelen.

define length_fact		if slope_r < 1 then (slope_length/72.6)**0.2 else if
						slope_r >=1 and slope_r < 3 then (slope_length/72.6)**0.3 else if
						slope_r >=3 and slope_r < 4.5 then (slope_length/72.6)**0.4 else if
						slope_r >= 4.5 then (slope_length/72.6)**0.5 else 0.

define sine_theta		sin(atan(slope_r/100)).
define steep_fact		(65.41)*(sine_theta**2)+(4.56*sine_theta)+0.065.
define ls_factor		(length_fact)*(steep_fact).

Computes the percentage of all rock fragments greater than 2mm in size in horizons with less than 35% total clay between 91 and 152cm.  Uses sieve and rock percents from the Horizon table.
 
The 2mm to 3" fragments are represented by the percent retained on the #10 sieve (100 - #10). This is adjusted for stones by multiplying it times the fraction less than 3" (1 - (Rock 3-10 + Rock >10)/100).

propname: SOC (kg/m2) to 1.5 m bedrock/duripan or petro* (NPS)
description:
Evaluates soil organic carbon (SOC) to a depth of two meters or to the occurrence of any type of bedrock or other certain types of restrictive layers. 


rev. SBSouthard 10/09
SBSouthard 3/2009

1. Soil organic carbon result is in kg/m2 to the depth of the soil.  Conversion to pounds/acre: (kg/m) X (2.2 lbs/kg) X (4047 m2/acre); so, kg/m X 8903 = pounds SOC/acre. Likewise, kg/m2 * 4.4515 = tons/acre.

2. This rule evaluates to 2 meter depth or to representative top depth of any bedrock kind, any petro horizon and any duripan. Other types of restrictions were not coded into the depth to restriction subproperty used in the main interpretation property script because the concern is not rooting depth restrictions but total amount of SOC stabilized in soils on a volumetric basis. It was decided to include stabilized soil organic carbon that may exist below a strongly contrasted particle size. In a Fluvent, for example, or buried old surfaces below tephra deposits there may be large stores of carbon that lie below other kinds of restrictive layers.

3. The calculation reports on a volumetric whole soil basis, corrected for representative rock fragments in database. The representative amount of soil passing the #10 sieve, rock fragment particle density, and the representative 1/3 bar density of the soil is given priority. If sieves and RF weights are NULL the rock fragment volume table is used instead. The soil organic carbon is converted from horizon soil organic matter content stored as a weight percent of the < 2mm fraction of the soil and recalculated on a whole soil basis. If soil organic matter in the database is NULL, SOC is assumed to be zero.

4. The NPS SOC class rule attached to this property was designed using an arbitrary linear curve in the associated evaluation. The curve was designed so that the "fuzzy value" multiplied by 1000 gives you that actual amount SOC calculated for the component in the NASIS data. Units are kg/meter2 to some depth when multiplied by 1000 for the rule.

Data issues:

1. NULL 1/3 bulk density may exist for mineral horizons and this calculation will assign a bulk density value of 0.2 because in most cases NULL 1/3 bulk density in the data occurs with O horizons. Using this assumption, in some cases the amount of SOC will be underestimated for non-organic horizons with no bulk density populated.

2. Particle densities vary over the country but 2.65 was used universally. More complex default queries could be written using parent material. It is not apparent if map results with broad SOC classes would reflect the extra effort to refine particle densities. This will result in either overestimation or underestimation of SOC depending on rock type. The property script can be copied and edited for particle densities for individual areas.

3. An alternative subproperty script was added in October 2009 to use the horizon rock fragment volume table instead of sieves if sieves, RF 3-10" and >10" data columns are NULL.

description:
Generates an ecological site name by combining the fields of the Ecological Site table into a string, which is returned in a variable named ecositenm. It requires the record id of the Ecological Site as a parameter. For example:

DERIVE ecositenm USING "NSSC Pangaea":"Ecological Site Name" (ecositeiid).

The rules for generating the name are:

If the Ecological Site Primary Name is non-blank, the Secondary and Tertiary names (if used) are appended to the Primary name with a space between each. This will be used as the output of the property.

If the Ecological Site Tree 1 is non-blank, the Tree, Shrub and Herb species are concantenated. If there are two trees the species names are combined with a hyphen, like "pine-spruce". If only one of the tree species is listed no hyphen is used. The pairs of shrub and herb species are combined the same way. Then the non-blank results of that step are combined with a slash "/" delimiter to produce the ecological site name. Examples are:

tree1-tree2/shrub1-shrub2/herb1-herb2
tree1/shrub1/herb1
tree1-tree2/shrub1

If both the Primary Name and Tree 1 columns have data, the corect form of the result cannot be determined and the result is set to "ambiguous name". If both columns are blank, even if other columns are filled in, the result is blank.

description:
Computes the thickness (in cm) of that portion of each horizon that is within a specified range, using the RV horizon depths.  Requires two parameters: the top and bottom depths (in cm) of the part of the profile to be examined.
This is normally called by another property that needs layer thickness.  It returns the results in the variable layer_thickness, which has one value for each horizon.

Finds the top depth of the first restrictive layer of any type.
Returns values for low, high, and rv: each has a single value.
Non-cemented restrictive features are excluded from the interpretations.

Data used: slope and slopelenusle_r from component table.
	Consideration:
	1. Slope
	2. "MLRA10_StPaul":"USLE SLOPE LENGTH (ND)" uses a look up table to assign slope length when slopelenusle_r is NULL.
		
Finds the "Slope-Length of Slope" index value from the following equation:
((0.065 + (0.0456 * slope_r) + (0.006541*(slope_r ** 2)))*((slopelenusle_r/22.1) ** mexp_r))

Where mexp_r is the slope exponent from the following list.
slope_r <1 then mexp_r = 0.2223
slope_r => 1 and <2 then mexp_r = 0.2684

Calculates the aggregate stablity for the 0 to 5 cm depth or to a restriction, whichever is first. Any thin organic layer present at the surface is removed.  The  weighted average aggregate stability is for that portion of each horizon in the depth range.

This property uses the methodology in the Web Soil Survey report named "Soil Health - Aggregate Stability (West US)" to calculate aggregate stability.

Aggregate stability is defined as the stability of macroaggregates (1-2 mm in size) against flowing water and is expressed as percent stable aggregates of the less than 2mm fraction. It is estimated from the organic matter content, total clay, and sodium adsorption ratio. Aggregate stability values are not calculated for sandy and organic surface layers.

Finds the flooding duration classes for all months.
Domain members are assigned a numeric value as follows:
Value	Name		Description
1	Extremely brief        0.1 to 4 hours
2	Very brief                4 hours to 48 hours
3	Brief                        2 days to 7 days
4	Long                        7 days to 30 days
5	Very long                 More than 30 days
 
Returns each distinct duration class in rv: multiple values are possible.

Finds the flooding frequency classes for all months.
Domain members are assigned a numeric value as follows:
Value	Name		Description
0	None	               No reasonable possibility of flooding; near 0 percent chance of flooding in any year or less than 1 time in 500 years.
1	Very rare	               Flooding is very unlikely but is possible under unusual weather conditions; less than 1 percent chance in any year (less than 1 time in 100 years, but more than 1 time in 500 years).
2	Rare	               Flooding is unlikely but possible under unusual weather conditions; 1 to 5 percent chance in any year (1 to 5 times in 100 years).
3	Occasional              Flooding is expected infrequently, 5 to 50 percent chance in any year, (5 to 50 times in 100 years).
4	Frequent	               Flooding is likely to occur often under usual weather conditions; more than 50 percent chance of flooding in any year or more than 50 times in 100 years, but less than a 50 percent chance of flooding in all months in any year.
5	Very frequent        Flooding is likey to occur very often under usual weather conditions; more than 50 percent chance in all months of any year.

Returns the MAX frequency class in rv.

propname: ID Hops WATER TABLE TOP DEPTH MIN MAR-OCT
description: This property returns the RV water table top depth (wet state) for the months of March through October.

Hops full range is 35 - 55 degrees latitude in both hemispheres, providing long summer days and moderately cool winters. However, locations between the 42nd and 49th parallel in the Northern Hemisphere are ideal and where the majority of the world's hop production is currently taking place.  This takes in all of Idaho, Oregon, and Washington, and most of Germany too.  Hops are a daylight sensitive crop, at the 49th parallel they get about 16 hours of sunlight at the maximum of summer solstice and about 15 hours at the 42nd. The shift from vegetative to regenerative growth occurs at a day length of 16 to 18 hours. However long periods of temperatures at 40 degrees C are not good for aroma development. 

Reference:
Haunold, Alfred. "Hops and hop growing." Soils, plant growth and crop production 2 (2010): 192-207.
Biendl, Martin, et al. Hops: Their cultivation, composition and usage. Fachverlag Hans Carl, 2015.

propname: DEPTH TO BULK DENSITY DIFFERENCE >.25 BELOW AN ORGANIC (ND)
description:
Bulk density above a "normal" level of compaction limits root growth.  This property calculates a theoretical ideal bulk density for that proportion of sand, silt, clay in the horizon.  The "ideal" bulk density is then subtracted from from the given bulk density.  If the difference is greater than  a calculated threshold, the layer has a root-limiting bulk density.

Reference: Pierce, F. J., W. E. Larson, R. H. Dowdy, and W. A. P. Graham.1983. Productivity of Soils: Assessing Long-term Changes Due to Erosion. J. Soil Water Conserv. 38:39-44.

The ratio of the difference between the observed bulk density and the "optimal" or "non-limiting" bulk density and the calculated difference between a limiting bulk density and a non-limiting bulk density at each combination of s, si, and c.  This is calculated by: delta=((0.002081*sandtotal_r)+(0.003912*silttotal_r)+0.044351).


Calculation:    ((dbthirdbar_r-(((sandtotal_r*1.65)/100)+((silttotal_r*1.40)/100)+((claytotal_r*1.30)/100))) > delta)

Assumptions:	The "ideal" bulk density for a sand is about 1.65 g/cm3
		The "ideal" bulk density for a silt is about 1.40 g/cm3
		The "ideal" bulk density for a clay is about 1.30 g/cm3

This property uses Hamon 1963 to find potential evapotranspiration.  It uses the Latitude Estimator to find the declination.  Mean annual air temperature is used in calculating the vapor pressure.  The monthly mean temperature  is estimated using the Latitude Estimator and Continentality.

Calculates an approximation of PET using Hamon (1963).

 PET= k*0.165*217.7*N*(es/(T+273.3))
 WHERE:
 PET= potential evapotranspiration [mm day-1]
 k= proportionality coefficient = 11 [unitless]
 N= daytime length [x/12 hours]
 N = (24/pi)*w
 es= saturation vapor pressure [mb]
 T= average monthly temperature [C]
 es = saturation vapor pressure
 es=6.108e(17.27T/(T+273.3))
 w = invcos(-tan(d)tan(phi))
 phi = latitude in radians
 d = declination in radians
 d= 1 + 0.033cos(2*pi*j/365)
 j is julian day of the year

exec sql select comonth.month
from component, comonth
where join component to comonth
and not exists(select * from cosoilmoist where soimoiststat = "wet" and join cosoilmoist to comonth
and (taxtempcl in ("hypergelic", "pergelic", "subgelic") 
and comonth.month in ("jul", "aug"))

or (taxtempregime in ("thermic")
and comonth.month in ("feb", "mar", "apr", "may", "jun", "jul", "aug", "sep", "oct"))

or (taxtempregime in ("mesic")
and comonth.month in ("mar", "apr", "may", "jun", "jul", "aug", "sep", "oct"))

or (taxtempregime in ("cryic")
and comonth.month in ("jun", "jul", "aug"))

or (taxtempregime in ("frigid", "isofrigid")
